items.title: The IBM PC's modest start
items.body: IBM announced its Personal Computer, model 5150, on 12 August 1981. It ran an Intel 8088 at 4.77 MHz, and the base model came with just 16 KB of memory. Because IBM published its technical details and used off-the-shelf parts, other companies could build compatible machines, which is why 'PC' became a whole category.
items.q: What processor did the original IBM PC use?
items.a: The Intel 8088, at 4.77 MHz.

items.title: Vachier-Lagrave unbeaten in Budapest's Group D
items.body: After four days of the Total Chess pilot in Budapest, Maxime Vachier-Lagrave was the only player without a loss in Group D, three points clear of Hans Niemann. Firouzja, Caruana and Martirosyan led the other three groups. Group play runs to 15 November, then knockouts follow after a rest day.

items.title: Thinking makes it so
items.body: There is nothing either good or bad, but thinking makes it so.

items.title: Hinted handoff: hold the note for a friend
items.body: In Dynamo-style stores like Cassandra, if a replica is down when a write arrives, another node accepts it and keeps a 'hint' saying who it was really for. When the missing node returns, the hint is replayed to it. Writes stay available during short outages, and the data finds its proper home later.
items.q: What does a node store during hinted handoff?
items.a: The write plus a hint naming the replica it was meant for, replayed when that replica returns.

items.title: Titan's seas of methane
items.body: Saturn's moon Titan is the only other world we know with stable liquid on its surface. It's far too cold for water to flow, so its lakes and seas are liquid methane and ethane. The largest, Kraken Mare, is bigger than the Caspian Sea, and Cassini radar mapped its shores.
items.hook: Wonder: what would rain look like on a world where it rains methane?

items.title: The Stroop effect
items.body: In 1935 J. Ridley Stroop showed that naming the ink colour of a word is slower when the word spells a different colour, like RED printed in blue. Reading is so automatic that it competes with the task you meant to do. It's a gentle reminder that well-practised habits run whether or not you ask them to.
items.q: Why is it slow to say 'blue' for the word RED printed in blue ink?
items.a: Reading the word is automatic and competes with naming the ink colour.

items.title: Let a character be wrong
items.body: Give a character one belief that is quietly mistaken: the neighbour is rude, the shortcut is faster, the letter was never sent. The reader enjoys sensing the gap, and the moment the character finds out becomes a ready-made turn in the story.
items.hook: Wonder: what were you once sure about that turned out not to be true?

items.title: How Indian numerals reached Europe
items.body: The digits 0 to 9 with place value were developed in India. Around 825 CE the Baghdad scholar al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on calculating with these 'Hindu numerals', and in 1202 Fibonacci's Liber Abaci showed European merchants how much easier they made sums than Roman numerals. Al-Khwarizmi's name also gave us the word 'algorithm'.
items.q: Which word in English comes from al-Khwarizmi's name?
items.a: Algorithm.

items.title: A gentle weekly look-ahead
items.body: Saturday or Sunday evening, spend fifteen minutes with the calendar for the coming week. Note one thing per day that needs preparing (a form, a bag, a charger) and put each on the day before. It's not a full plan, just fewer surprises on Monday.
items.hook: Wonder: what's one thing next week that would be easier if you set it out tonight?

items.title: Google's agent teams that check their own work
items.body: Google Research described Antigravity /teamwork, where several specialised Gemini 4 agents tackle open problems in maths and information theory. Each agent sees only the context it needs, and proposed answers go to 'falsifiers' such as the Lean 4 proof checker before anything is accepted. Google is opening the tools to outside researchers.
items.q: What role does Lean 4 play in Antigravity /teamwork?
items.a: It acts as a falsifier, checking candidate solutions before they're accepted.

items.title: Shouldering: use your king as a wall
items.body: In king endgames, the king can block the enemy king with its own body. Instead of racing straight for a pawn, step sideways or diagonally so the other king has to go around you. Those one or two lost tempi often decide whether a pawn queens or is caught.
items.hook: Wonder: when is the fastest route not a straight line?

items.title: Skip lists: a linked list with express lanes
items.body: A skip list keeps sorted items in a linked list, then adds sparser 'express' levels above it, each node promoted by a coin flip. Searches ride the top lane and drop down as they get close, giving about O(log n) lookups without the rotations of a balanced tree. Redis uses skip lists for its sorted sets.
items.q: How does a skip list decide which nodes get an express-lane level?
items.a: Randomly, like a coin flip for each level.

items.title: While we postpone
items.body: While we are postponing, life speeds by.
items.who: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius, Letter 1 (tr. Gummere)

items.title: Could dark energy once have been negative?
items.body: Researchers at Istanbul Technical University explored a branch of a modified-gravity theory in which dark energy's effective density starts out negative in the early universe and crosses zero about 9.5 billion years ago. It's a theoretical model, not a finding: the authors note it still has to be tested against the full DESI survey data.
items.hook: Wonder: how do astronomers 'look back' 9.5 billion years at all?

items.title: Dijkstra's twenty-minute algorithm
items.body: In 1956 Edsger Dijkstra was shopping in Amsterdam with his fiancée, sat down at a café terrace, and worked out his shortest-path algorithm in about twenty minutes, without pencil or paper. He later said avoiding paper forced him to keep it simple. It was published in 1959 and still guides route-finding today.
items.q: Where did Dijkstra design his shortest-path algorithm?
items.a: At a café terrace in Amsterdam, in about twenty minutes, without paper.

items.title: The bookstall's last customer
items.body: At closing time the boy still stood by the comics, counting coins he did not have enough of. The old bookseller pulled the shutter halfway, then said he needed someone to check whether issue 12 had all its pages. The boy checked, carefully, every page. 'Good,' said the bookseller. 'Inspectors get paid in copies.'

items.title: 'Muscle' means 'little mouse'
items.body: The word muscle comes from the Latin musculus, 'little mouse'. Romans apparently thought a flexing muscle under the skin looked like a small mouse moving about.
items.hook: Wonder: which other body words hide an animal?

items.title: A DNS-style address book for agents
items.body: The Agent Name Service (ANS) is now a Linux Foundation project. It gives AI agents verifiable identities using DNS records tied to a domain plus certificates, so one agent can check that another really belongs to the organisation it claims. Eleven organisations are listed as early supporters.
items.hook: Wonder: how does your browser already know a website is who it says it is?

items.title: Write the worry down before the test
items.body: In a 2011 study in Science, Gerardo Ramirez and Sian Beilock had students spend ten minutes writing about their worries just before an exam. Anxious students who did this scored better than those who sat quietly. One idea: putting the worry on paper frees working memory that would otherwise be busy holding it.
items.q: What did students do for ten minutes before the exam in Ramirez and Beilock's study?
items.a: Wrote freely about their worries about the test.

items.title: The big temple's tower at Thanjavur
items.body: Rajaraja Chola I completed the Brihadisvara temple in Thanjavur around 1010 CE. Its tower rises about 66 metres and is built largely of granite, a stone not found close to the city, so huge blocks had to be brought in from elsewhere. It is part of UNESCO's 'Great Living Chola Temples', and worship there has continued for over a thousand years.
items.q: Roughly when was Thanjavur's Brihadisvara temple completed?
items.a: Around 1010 CE, under Rajaraja Chola I.

items.title: A ten-minute warning
items.body: Switching away from something absorbing is often the hard part, not the next task itself. Set a soft alarm ten minutes before you need to stop, labelled with what comes next. The early nudge lets you find a natural pause instead of being yanked out mid-thought.
items.hook: Wonder: which transition in your day is the bumpiest?

items.title: Andreikin nearly sweeps the 3|0 Thursdays
items.body: Chess.com runs three 3-minute 'Thursday' tournaments each week. On 12 November GM Dmitry Andreikin won two of them and finished half a point short of taking the third, the closest anyone has come to winning all three in one week.
items.hook: Wonder: what keeps a blitz player steady across three tournaments in one day?

items.title: Java 22: say 'I don't need this' with _
items.body: Since Java 22, an underscore can stand in for a variable you must declare but never use: catch (NumberFormatException _) { ... }, or a lambda like (k, _) -> k. It also works inside record patterns, e.g. case Point(var x, _) -> x. The code now tells the reader, and the compiler, that ignoring the value is deliberate.
items.q: Which Java version finalised unnamed variables with _?
items.a: Java 22 (JEP 456).

items.title: A 'digital twin' of Webb finds a planet in old data
items.body: A Caltech-led team published a method called FLIP in Nature. It builds a detailed computer model of Webb's NIRCam camera so the starlight around a bright star can be subtracted more cleanly. In tests it was 2 to 15 times more sensitive, and it uncovered a planet that had been sitting unnoticed in images Webb had already taken.
items.q: What does the FLIP method model in order to remove starlight?
items.a: Webb's own NIRCam instrument, as a detailed 'digital twin'.

items.title: Saturday, half past ten
items.body:
The street has put its shoes away.
One window keeps a yellow square.
The kettle ticks as it cools down,
and the week, folded, rests on a chair.

items.title: Rivals team up on one open inference engine
items.body: LMSYS announced an SGLang Consortium that brings NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Google, Meta, Cloudflare, Modal and RadixArk together to steer the open-source SGLang serving engine across different hardware. No new version or benchmark came with it; the news is simply that chip makers who usually compete will coordinate on one shared piece of plumbing.
items.hook: Wonder: why might competitors happily share the 'boring' layer of a stack?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try answering before you peek. Pulling an answer out of memory strengthens it more than re-reading does.
items.q: 1) What did Perseverance confirm in old Mars rocks? 2) What does compaction do in an LSM tree? 3) Who won Freestyle Friday on 13 November?
items.a: 1) Complex organic carbon just below the surface. 2) Merges sorted on-disk files so reads touch fewer of them. 3) IM Khuong Duy Dau, 15, of Vietnam.

items.title: An ostrich's eye outweighs its brain
items.body: An ostrich's eye is about 5 cm across, among the largest of any land animal, and each eye is bigger than its brain. Those huge eyes help it spot movement across open plains from a long way off.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you notice if your eyes were the biggest thing in your head?

items.title: The quality of mercy
items.body:
The quality of mercy is not strain'd,
It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven
Upon the place beneath: it is twice blest;
It blesseth him that gives and him that takes.

items.title: VS Code 1.146 helps you juggle many agents
items.body: Microsoft's VS Code 1.146 adds tools for managing many agent sessions at once, so you can keep several parallel tasks visible instead of losing track of them in tabs. The release also starts a three-month countdown to retire the older Local agent harness, while the Copilot harness stays and keeps getting work.
items.q: What's being retired in VS Code over the next three months?
items.a: The Local agent harness (the Copilot harness stays).

items.title: Ethernet began as a memo
items.body: On 22 May 1973, Bob Metcalfe at Xerox PARC wrote a memo describing a way for computers in a building to share one cable and politely take turns talking. He called it Ethernet, borrowing the old idea of the 'luminiferous ether'. Versions of that idea still carry much of the world's local network traffic.
items.hook: Wonder: what everyday technology around you started as a single page someone wrote?

items.title: The windmill
items.body: A windmill is a repeating discovered check: one piece shuttles back and forth, uncovering check each time and grabbing material on every swing while the king can only step aside. The most famous one came in Carlos Torre's win over Emanuel Lasker at Moscow 1925, where Torre's rook and bishop worked together to sweep up piece after piece.
items.q: Which two players featured in the famous 1925 windmill game?
items.a: Carlos Torre (winning) against Emanuel Lasker, Moscow 1925.

items.title: Fourteenth of November
items.body:
The calendar says Saturday
the way a door says open.

Nothing urgent lives here.
Just a window,
a fan turning slow enough to count,
and the whole long afternoon
folded like a towel,
waiting.

items.title: Raft leader election, in one breath
items.body: In Raft, every node starts as a follower listening for heartbeats from a leader. If a follower hears nothing for a randomised timeout, it becomes a candidate, bumps the term number and asks others for votes. A majority makes it leader. The randomness is the clever bit: it makes it unlikely that two nodes stand for election at exactly the same moment, so ties settle quickly.
items.q: Why are Raft election timeouts randomised?
items.a: So nodes rarely become candidates at the same moment, which avoids repeated split votes.

items.title: Sunlight's long walk out of the Sun
items.body: The light reaching you took about eight minutes to cross space, but its energy spent far longer inside the Sun. Near the core, energy is absorbed and re-emitted countless times, wandering outward in a random walk. Estimates for that journey range from tens of thousands of years to far longer.
items.hook: Wonder: how old is the warmth on your skin this morning, really?

items.title: Hang the new habit on an old one
items.body: New routines stick better when they ride on something you already do without thinking. 'After I switch on the kettle, I'll take my tablets.' 'After I close the laptop, I'll write tomorrow's first task.' The old habit becomes the reminder, so your memory doesn't have to be.
items.hook: Wonder: which three things do you already do every single day that could carry a passenger?

items.title: The # has a name: octothorpe
items.body: The # symbol is called the octothorpe, a name usually traced to engineers at Bell Labs in the early 1960s, when the symbol was being added to telephone keypads. The 'octo' part points to its eight ends; the 'thorpe' part has several competing origin stories, and nobody is quite sure which is true.
items.q: What is the formal name for the # symbol?
items.a: The octothorpe.

items.title: Willpower isn't a fuel tank (probably)
items.body: 'Ego depletion', the idea that self-control runs out like fuel, was popular for years. Then large, carefully planned replications across many labs found little or no effect. A kinder reading of the evidence: tiredness and boredom are real, but you're not a battery that hits zero. Rest, interest and good setup matter more than rationing yourself.
items.hook: Wonder: which 'facts' about your own mind would you hold more loosely if they failed a replication?

items.title: Bhimbetka's painted shelters
items.body: In the forested hills of Madhya Pradesh, the rock shelters of Bhimbetka hold paintings of animals, dancers, hunters and riders. Some are thought to be around 10,000 years old, and people kept adding to the walls over many later periods. The site was recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 2003.
items.q: In which Indian state are the Bhimbetka rock shelters?
items.a: Madhya Pradesh.

items.title: AWS gives agent runtimes their own sealed rooms
items.body: Amazon updated the runtime behind Bedrock AgentCore for long-running, multi-step agent work. Each session gets hardware-level isolation, starts faster and has more compute, and billing follows actual usage rather than reserved capacity, which suits agents that sit idle while waiting on a tool.
items.hook: Wonder: why does an agent that 'waits' a lot need different pricing from a web server?

items.title: Fix the verb, drop the adverb
items.body: 'She walked slowly' asks two words to do one job. 'She ambled', 'she trudged', 'she drifted' each carry a different mood in a single word. When you spot an adverb leaning on a verb, try swapping in a stronger verb. Keep the adverb only when it adds something the verb can't.
items.q: What's a one-word alternative to 'walked slowly' that adds mood?
items.a: Any precise verb, e.g. ambled, trudged, drifted, strolled.

items.title: A 15-year-old wins Freestyle Friday
items.body: International Master Khuong Duy Dau, a 15-year-old from Vietnam, won Chess.com's Freestyle Friday on 13 November, finishing a clear 1.5 points ahead of second place. Freestyle (Chess960) shuffles the back-rank pieces, so memorised openings help much less and fresh thinking from move one is rewarded.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your skills would survive if the 'starting position' of your work were shuffled?

items.title: Java 11: String.repeat
items.body: Need a divider line or some padding? Since Java 11, "-".repeat(40) gives you forty dashes, no loop or StringBuilder needed. repeat(0) returns an empty string, and a negative count throws IllegalArgumentException.
items.q: What does "ab".repeat(3) return?
items.a: "ababab"

items.title: First, who you would be
items.body: First say to yourself what you would be; and then do what you have to do.

items.title: ELIZA, the 1966 conversation
items.body: In the mid-1960s at MIT, Joseph Weizenbaum wrote ELIZA, a program that chatted by matching patterns and reflecting your words back, most famously in a 'DOCTOR' script that imitated a gentle therapist. It understood nothing, yet people found talking to it surprisingly absorbing. Weizenbaum himself became one of the first thoughtful voices asking how we should relate to machines that seem to listen.
items.hook: Wonder: why does being heard feel real even when we know the listener is simple?

items.title: A white dwarf that ticks every 7.9 minutes
items.body: Astronomers from Curtin University and ICRAR found a white dwarf sending out radio pulses every 7.9 minutes while it orbits a Sun-like star. It's the first time this kind of slow, repeating radio signal has been traced to a white dwarf paired with a Sun-like partner, and the pulses seem to carry hints of activity on the companion star. The system goes by GPM J071507-114153.
items.q: How often does this white dwarf's radio signal repeat?
items.a: About every 7.9 minutes.

items.title: The library's returns slot
items.body:
Every night at closing, Meera emptied the returns slot. Most books came back silent. Some came back with things inside: a bus ticket, a pressed neem leaf, a shopping list that said only 'eggs, patience'.

She kept the list. Over the years she found it again three times, in three different books, in three different hands.

She never learned who wrote it first. She just bought eggs, and practised the other thing.

items.title: Goats see in widescreen
items.body: Goats, sheep and many other grazing animals have horizontal, rectangular pupils. The shape gives them a wide panoramic view of the ground around them, and remarkably, their eyes rotate as they lower their heads to graze so the pupils stay level with the horizon.
items.hook: Wonder: what would your day look like with nearly all-round vision?

items.title: Look at the target, not your elbow
items.body: In motor learning, Gabriele Wulf and colleagues found again and again that people learn and perform better with an external focus (the path of the ball, the target, the effect of the movement) than an internal one (what the wrist or elbow is doing). Thinking about body parts tends to make movement stiffer. Coaches now often phrase cues outward: 'push the floor away' rather than 'straighten your knees'.
items.q: Which usually works better for skilled movement: focus on your body, or on the movement's effect?
items.a: On the effect (an external focus).

items.title: n8n opens up Nod, a personal agent that runs on your machine
items.body: n8n Labs released Nod as open source under the Apache 2.0 licence. It's a personal automation agent that runs locally on a Mac, Windows PC or private server, works inside a sandboxed browser and desktop, and lets you pick which model powers it. The examples are pleasantly ordinary: preparing for a meeting, filing invoices, cancelling a subscription.
items.q: What licence did n8n use for Nod?
items.a: Apache 2.0.

items.title: Kamban's Ramayana
items.body: Around the 12th century, the Tamil poet Kambar retold the Ramayana in Tamil verse. The Kamba Ramayanam isn't a translation of Valmiki: it reshapes scenes, lingers on landscapes and emotions, and is loved for its music. A Tamil saying holds that even the loom in Kambar's house could sing verse.
items.hook: Wonder: when a story is retold in a new language, how much of it becomes the new teller's?

items.title: Start with a warm-up task
items.body: 'Eat the frog first' doesn't suit every brain. If starting is the hard part, begin with a tiny task you can finish in five minutes: reply to one message, rename one file. A quick win builds momentum, and momentum is easier to steer toward the big task than a cold start is. Just choose the warm-up in advance so it doesn't become the whole morning.
items.q: What's the one guardrail for using a warm-up task?
items.a: Pick it in advance and keep it tiny, so it leads into the main task instead of replacing it.

items.title: Caruana touches 2800 in Budapest
items.body: On day four of the Total Chess pilot in Budapest, Fabiano Caruana beat Vincent Keymer and climbed to 2800.0 on the live rating list. The same day Magnus Carlsen lost to Haik Martirosyan, a reminder that even long reigns at the top are made of ordinary, winnable games. Group play continues through 15 November.
items.hook: Wonder: what does a rating number actually measure, a person or a recent run of games?

items.title: LSM trees: write fast, tidy later
items.body: Many databases (Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB) use a log-structured merge tree. New writes go into a sorted in-memory table; when it fills, it's flushed to disk as an immutable sorted file. In the background, files are merged ('compaction') so reads don't have to check too many of them. The trade: writes are cheap and sequential, reads may touch several files, and compaction quietly does the housekeeping.
items.q: In an LSM tree, what background process keeps reads from checking too many files?
items.a: Compaction: merging the sorted on-disk files together.

items.title: Perseverance confirms organic carbon in old Mars rocks
items.body: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon sitting just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks. Organic carbon isn't a sign of life by itself, but it is one of the ingredients scientists hope to find, and rocks that kept it safe for billions of years are exactly the kind worth bringing home one day.
items.q: Does finding organic carbon on Mars prove there was life there?
items.a: No. It's an ingredient for life, not proof of it; it can also form without biology.

items.title: Saturday, slow tea
items.body:
No alarm today.
The light finds the kitchen first,
then the steel tumbler,
then me.

The tea takes its time.
So do I.
Somewhere a crow is reading the morning aloud
and nobody is asking it to hurry.

items.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen becomes Google's fast default
items.body: Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a quick, low-cost model that takes over from Gemini 3.8 Flash as the go-to choice for high-volume work, with coding agents in mind. It adds an extra 'xhigh' thinking level above the existing ones, and it showed up the same day inside Google's Antigravity editor alongside a mode that can hand a task between models mid-run.
items.hook: Wonder: when a 'small' model gets good enough, what do you stop sending to the big one?

items.title: An 85-letter hill
items.body: A hill in New Zealand's Hawke's Bay carries one of the longest place names in the world: an 85-letter Māori name usually shortened to Taumata. It honours a traveller named Tamatea, who is said to have played his flute there.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you name a hill after something you did there?

items.title: Rice drying on the terrace
items.body:
Spread thin on an old sari,
the grains take the sun
one by one,
while a crow considers
and decides, for now,
to be patient too.

items.title: Head-of-line blocking
items.body: When requests share one ordered line, a single slow one holds up everything behind it, even the quick ones. That's head-of-line blocking. HTTP/2 fixed it at the request level by multiplexing streams over one connection, and HTTP/3 (over QUIC) fixed it at the transport level, so one lost packet only stalls its own stream.
items.q: What does HTTP/3 change so one lost packet doesn't stall every stream?
items.a: It runs over QUIC, where each stream is delivered independently.

items.title: Such stuff as dreams
items.body:
We are such stuff
As dreams are made on, and our little life
Is rounded with a sleep.

items.title: The Réti manoeuvre: chase two goals at once
items.body:
In Richard Réti's 1921 study, White's king looks hopelessly far from Black's runaway pawn. But by walking diagonally, the king moves towards the enemy pawn and towards supporting its own pawn at the same time. Black can't stop both ideas, and the game is drawn.

The lesson: on a chessboard, a diagonal walk is as short as a straight one.
items.hook: Wonder: where in life does one move serve two goals?

items.title: The Memex, a 1945 dream of linked documents
items.body: In his 1945 essay 'As We May Think', engineer Vannevar Bush imagined a desk called the Memex that stored a person's books and notes on microfilm and let them build 'trails' linking one document to another. Decades later, hypertext pioneers cited it as an inspiration for the web's links.
items.hook: Wonder: what would your own trail of linked notes look like?

items.title: Let the trained hands work
items.body: When a skill is well learned, watching every step too closely can make it worse. Studies of skilled golfers and typists found that focusing on the mechanics under pressure disrupted fluent performance, while a simple outward focus, like the target or a single word, helped it flow.
items.q: Why can thinking hard about each step hurt a well-practised skill?
items.a: It disrupts the automatic, fluent control that practice built; an outward focus helps it run smoothly.

items.title: Give the side character an errand
items.body: A minor character feels real the moment they want something unrelated to the hero: the shopkeeper needs to close early for a wedding, the friend is hunting for a lost charger. One line of their own small errand makes the world feel busy and alive beyond the main plot.
items.hook: Wonder: what is the most minor person in your story trying to get done today?

items.title: The Sun gets a little lighter every second
items.body: Fusion in the Sun's core turns mass into energy, about four million tonnes every second. It sounds enormous, but the Sun is so vast that over its whole life so far it has lost only a tiny fraction of a percent of its mass this way.
items.hook: Wonder: the sunlight on your face was, a moment ago, a little bit of the Sun's weight.

items.title: Pamban Bridge, India's first sea bridge
items.body: Opened in 1914, the Pamban railway bridge carried trains across the sea to Rameswaram island, making it India's first sea bridge. Its middle section was a lift span whose two halves rolled upward to let ships pass beneath.
items.q: What made the old Pamban Bridge special when it opened in 1914?
items.a: It was India's first sea bridge, with a middle span that opened upward for ships.

items.title: Write the 'why' next to the 'what'
items.body: A task like 'email Priya' is easy to skip; 'email Priya so the trip dates are settled' carries its own reason. Adding a few words of why gives your brain the interest and meaning it needs to start, and makes it clearer which tasks can quietly be dropped.
items.hook: Wonder: which item on your list has no reason left?

items.title: Anthropic: one shared agent beat many personal ones
items.body: Anthropic's alignment team tested frontier models in four multi-agent settings where several people had to share an outcome. In every setting, the group did worse when each person had their own agent than when one shared agent served everyone. Three of the test environments are released as a benchmark, MAMUBench.
items.q: In Anthropic's 'Worse Together' study, which setup gave better group outcomes?
items.a: One shared agent serving everyone, rather than one agent per person.

items.title: The see-through frog
items.body: Glass frogs have translucent bellies, so you can see their organs from below. While they sleep, some species go a step further: they tuck most of their red blood cells away in the liver, which makes their bodies even more transparent.
items.hook: Wonder: what else in nature hides by becoming clearer rather than darker?

items.title: Java 16: Stream.toList()
items.body:
Since Java 16 you can write list.stream().filter(...).toList() instead of .collect(Collectors.toList()). It's shorter, and the result is unmodifiable: calling add() on it throws UnsupportedOperationException.

Need a list you can change later? Keep using Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new).
items.q: Can you add elements to the list returned by Stream.toList()?
items.a: No, it's unmodifiable; adding throws UnsupportedOperationException.

items.title: The radio repairman's quiet
items.body:
Every radio that came into Selvam's shop got the same first test: he switched it on and listened to the hiss for a full minute. Customers fidgeted. 'The hiss tells me more than the music,' he'd say.

One evening a boy brought a radio that worked perfectly. 'My grandfather listened to it,' he said. 'I just wanted someone to hear it with.' Selvam turned it on, and they listened to the hiss together for a full minute, and then the news of rain, and then a song neither of them knew.

items.title: The Saavedra position
items.body:
A famous endgame from 1895: White has a pawn about to promote against a lone rook. Making a queen sounds obvious, but Black has a trick that leads to stalemate. Promoting to a rook instead dodges the stalemate, and White wins with a double threat a move later.

It's one of the loveliest reminders that the 'best' piece isn't always the right one.
items.q: What does White promote to in the Saavedra position?
items.a: A rook, because a queen would allow a stalemate defence.

items.title: Put the label on the picture
items.body: When a diagram's labels sit in a separate legend, your eyes bounce back and forth and your working memory does the stitching. Researchers call this the split-attention effect. Placing each label right on the part it names, or the explanation next to the step it explains, makes the same material easier to learn.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your own notes would get easier if the words moved closer to the picture?

items.title: The Easter egg in Adventure
items.body: Warren Robinett hid a secret room in Adventure, his 1980 game for the Atari 2600, with the words 'Created by Warren Robinett'. Atari didn't credit its programmers at the time, so he signed his work in secret. It's one of the most famous early video-game Easter eggs, and it helped the term catch on.
items.q: Why did Warren Robinett hide his name inside Adventure?
items.a: Atari didn't credit programmers, so he signed the game in a secret room.

items.title: Clean within
items.body: Keep the mind free of stain: that alone is virtue. Everything else is only noise.

items.title: A 'supernova impostor' finally explained
items.body: For years, an object called AT 2016blu in the galaxy NGC 4559 kept flaring as if a star were exploding, yet the star never died. Astronomers now think a hidden companion, a black hole or neutron star, is feeding on an unstable massive star, and each feeding spell sets off an outburst that mimics a supernova.
items.hook: Wonder: how many 'explosions' in the sky are really long conversations between two stars?

items.title: Manimekalai, the epic that came next
items.body: Manimekalai, one of the five great epics of Tamil literature, is often read as a sequel to Silappatikaram. Its heroine is the daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi, and her story follows a quieter path, towards learning, compassion and a begging bowl that never empties. It is traditionally credited to the poet Sattanar.
items.hook: Wonder: what would it be like to write the sequel to someone else's famous story?

items.title: MCP and Agent Skills grow up in the open
items.body: Google's open-source blog describes how the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent Skills are now maintained under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, with Google Cloud engineers among the co-maintainers. The aim is a shared, open way to give agents tools and context, so one integration works across many agents.
items.q: Which foundation now hosts MCP and Agent Skills?
items.a: The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), part of the Linux Foundation.

items.title: Apples float
items.body: Apples float in water because roughly a quarter of their volume is air, trapped between their cells. That's why apple bobbing works at all.
items.q: Why do apples float?
items.a: About a quarter of an apple's volume is air trapped between its cells.

items.title: A five-minute Friday shutdown
items.body:
Before the weekend, spend five minutes closing loops: jot down what's half-done, where you left it, and the very next step for Monday. Then close the tabs.

Monday-you gets a map instead of a fog, and weekend-you doesn't have to keep carrying it.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the one line Monday-you would most like to find?

items.title: Vallejo opens with three wins in Salamanca
items.body: Paco Vallejo started the Salamanca Masters with a perfect 3/3, beating Anastasiia Hnatyshyn, José Martínez and Loek van Wely to take the sole lead. Martínez is second on 2/3. Eleven-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan bounced back from two early losses to beat Elisabeth Paehtz in round three.

items.title: Event sourcing: keep the story, not just the ending
items.body:
Most databases store only the current state: balance = 420. Event sourcing stores every change instead: deposited 500, paid 80. The current state is just the events replayed in order.

You get a full history for free, can rebuild views later, and can answer 'how did we get here?'. The cost: replays get slow, so systems save periodic snapshots and replay only the events after them.
items.q: In event sourcing, how is the current state of an account produced?
items.a: By replaying its stored events in order, usually starting from the latest snapshot.

items.title: Friday, the late lamp
items.body:
The week folds itself
like a shirt nobody asked to iron.
One lamp stays on in the hall,
not for work,
just so the stairs remember
where they go.
items.hook: Wonder: what small light do you leave on for yourself?

items.title: Earth's water may be homemade
items.body: A new study suggests some of Earth's water may not have arrived on comets or asteroids at all. In lab conditions, hot rocky material reacting with hydrogen produced water, hinting that the young Earth's fiery early atmosphere could have made a large amount of its own, possibly many oceans' worth.
items.hook: Wonder: the water in your glass might have been cooked up by the young planet itself.

items.title: Databricks' Genie can keep working in the background
items.body: Databricks has introduced an always-on mode for Genie, its data agent. Instead of waiting for each question, it can run in the background, pull together company information and take on longer assignments. A new 'Ontology' feature maps how people, projects and data relate to each other. The always-on mode is heading to preview first.
items.hook: Wonder: what's one slow, repetitive question you'd hand to a background helper?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Before you scroll, a warm-up: a few small questions from this edition are waiting further down. Try answering each before you peek.
items.q: In the Saavedra position, why does White promote to a rook instead of a queen?
items.a: A new queen allows a stalemate trick; the rook avoids stalemate and still wins.

items.title: A Mars day is a little longer
items.body: A solar day on Mars, called a sol, lasts about 24 hours and 40 minutes. Mission teams on Earth who live on Mars time shift their schedules about 40 minutes later each day.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you do with an extra 40 minutes every day?

items.title: The postman's bicycle
items.body:
Its bell has one opinion,
its basket holds the town:
a birthday, a bill, a postcard
from someone's sister in Kodaikanal,
all leaning on each other
on the long ride down.

items.title: Sliding-window rate limits
items.body:
A fixed-window limiter ('100 requests per minute, resetting at :00') lets bursts slip through at the boundary: 100 at 0:59, another 100 at 1:00. A sliding window counts requests over the last 60 seconds from right now, so the limit holds smoothly.

A cheap version blends the current and previous window's counts, weighted by how far into the current window you are.
items.q: What weakness of fixed-window rate limiting does a sliding window fix?
items.a: Bursts at window boundaries, where a client can send almost double the limit in a short span.

items.title: Answer harm with kindness
items.body: To answer those who hurt you, do them good, until they feel ashamed; then let both the hurt and the kindness be forgotten.

items.title: Nakamura stays with Chess.com
items.body: Hikaru Nakamura has signed a new long-term agreement with Chess.com, extending a partnership that began in 2013. He'll join the commentary team for some key games of the upcoming World Championship match, and a 'Hikaru vs. The World' event is planned for 2027.

items.title: Let the agent ask one question
items.body:
When you hand an agent a task, allow it exactly one clarifying question before it starts. One question forces it to find the biggest gap in your request, without turning the job into an interview.

Often the question itself shows you what you forgot to say.
items.hook: Wonder: what would your most-asked clarifying question be?

items.title: Flow lives at the edge of skill
items.body:
Psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi found that deep absorption, which he called flow, tends to appear when a task's challenge sits just above your current skill. Too easy and you drift into boredom; too hard and you tense up.

If you're bored, add a constraint. If you're anxious, shrink the step.

items.title: Tetris began in Moscow, 1984
items.body: Alexey Pajitnov wrote the first Tetris in June 1984 on an Elektronika 60 computer at the Soviet Academy of Sciences. The name blends 'tetromino' (a shape of four squares) and 'tennis', his favourite sport.
items.q: Which two words were blended to make the name 'Tetris'?
items.a: Tetromino and tennis.

items.title: A hidden twist in the solar wind
items.body: Using Parker Solar Probe data, an international team found that turbulent magnetic fields in the solar wind flip their direction of rotation at very small scales. The flip happens where the plasma stops acting like a fluid and starts acting like individual particles, a clue that could help improve space-weather forecasts.

items.title: Give big tasks a progress bar
items.body:
Long tasks feel endless because you can't see them moving. Split one into 10 pieces and draw 10 empty boxes on a sticky note. Fill a box each time a piece is done.

Watching the bar fill gives your brain the steady small rewards it likes.

items.title: Charminar, 1591
items.body: Hyderabad's Charminar ('four minarets') was built in 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, the Qutb Shahi ruler who founded the city. It stood at the heart of the new city's layout, and its upper floor holds a small mosque.
items.hook: Wonder: what does a city choose to put at its very centre?

items.title: Give the reader a small mystery early
items.body: Plant one unexplained detail in the first lines: a locked drawer, a name no one says, a coat that's too big. You don't need a big secret. A small open question gives the reader a reason to keep going, and answering it later feels like a reward.

items.title: The far side isn't dark
items.body: The side of the Moon we never see from Earth gets just as much sunlight as the side we do. 'Dark side' only meant unknown. During our new Moon, the far side is in full daylight.
items.q: When the Moon is 'new' for us, what is the far side doing?
items.a: Basking in full sunlight.

items.title: Google Labs tries Tabletop
items.body: Google Labs opened a waitlist for Tabletop, an experiment that builds small shared spaces from a prompt: a trip plan, a shared expense tracker, a dinner poll or a tournament bracket. Friends can join and edit together in real time. For now it's limited to adults in the US.

items.title: Canary releases
items.body:
Instead of shipping a new version to everyone at once, send it to a small slice of traffic first, say 1%. Watch error rates and latency. If it behaves, widen the slice step by step; if not, roll back while most users never noticed.

The name comes from the canaries miners once carried as an early warning.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the smallest audience that would still tell you something true?

items.title: Zugzwang: when moving hurts
items.body: Zugzwang is German for 'compulsion to move'. It describes a position where you'd be fine if you could pass, but every legal move makes things worse. It shows up most in king-and-pawn endings, where one spare tempo can decide the game.
items.q: In which kind of position does zugzwang show up most often?
items.a: Endgames, especially king-and-pawn endings.

items.title: Running with the stars
items.body: Look round at the courses of the stars, as if thou wert going along with them.

items.title: Lumina: watching the first light spread
items.body: MIT and Harvard researchers built a huge supercomputer simulation, called Lumina, that follows 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region about 1.6 billion light-years wide. It shows how the first stars, galaxies and black holes slowly lit up and re-ionized the hydrogen and helium filling the young universe.
items.hook: Wonder: what did the universe look like the moment its first stars switched on?

items.title: The ticket inspector's sums
items.body:
On the 7:10 local, the inspector never punched tickets right away. He asked each child on the way to school one sum. Seven eights. Twelve plus nineteen. A girl by the window got hers wrong every morning for a month, and every morning he said, 'Tomorrow, then.'

In March she held out her ticket and said, 'Fifty-six, before you ask.' He punched it with a little flourish, like a stamp in a passport.

items.title: Git was written in a hurry
items.body: In April 2005, after Linux lost free use of the BitKeeper tool, Linus Torvalds started writing Git. Within days it was tracking its own source code. A few months later he handed it to Junio Hamano, who has maintained it ever since.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you build if you only had a couple of weeks and a clear need?

items.title: The fresh start effect
items.body:
People are more likely to begin a new goal on a calendar landmark: a Monday, the first of the month, a birthday. Researchers Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman and Jason Riis called this the fresh start effect (2014).

You don't have to wait for one, though. You can draw your own line: 'After this cup of tea, a new chapter.'
items.q: What do we call the boost in motivation people feel on dates like Mondays or birthdays?
items.a: The fresh start effect.

items.title: There's no lead in a pencil
items.body: Pencil 'lead' is graphite mixed with clay. Early users mistook graphite for a kind of lead ore, and the name stuck. Pencils have never had lead in their cores.
items.hook: Wonder: how many everyday names are leftover mistakes?

items.title: A local AWS stand-in, written by agents
items.body: Amazon released a free local tool that simulates more than 200 AWS services, so developers can test cloud code on their own machine. Amazon says AI agents wrote and maintain all of its code. It notes the emulator doesn't fully copy every real-world limit, such as service restrictions.

items.title: Kodumanal, a Sangam-age workshop town
items.body: Near the Noyyal river in Tamil Nadu's Erode district, excavations at Kodumanal have found an ancient craft centre: beads of beryl, quartz and carnelian, evidence of iron and steel working, and potsherds scratched with Tamil-Brahmi letters. Sangam poetry seems to remember it as Kodumanam.
items.q: Which river does the ancient craft town of Kodumanal sit near?
items.a: The Noyyal, in Erode district, Tamil Nadu.

items.title: Count up, not down
items.body:
A countdown timer can feel like a ticking alarm. Try a stopwatch that counts up instead. It quietly shows how long you've been at something, so time becomes visible without the pressure of a deadline.

When you stop, glance at it: 'I did 14 minutes.' That's a small, honest win.
items.hook: Wonder: does your focus change when time feels like a tally rather than a fuse?

items.title: Caruana and Niemann sweep in Budapest
items.body: Day 3 of the Total Chess World Championship Tour pilot belonged to two players who won both their games. Fabiano Caruana beat Praggnanandhaa twice and leads Group B with 10 points; Hans Niemann beat Vaishali twice to share the Group D lead with Maxime Vachier-Lagrave. Bibisara Assaubayeva also earned a career-best win over Arjun Erigaisi in one of their games.

items.title: Java 21: getFirst, getLast, reversed
items.body:
Java 21 added sequenced collections (JEP 431). List, Deque and LinkedHashSet now share methods like getFirst(), getLast(), addFirst(), removeLast() and reversed().

So list.get(list.size() - 1) becomes list.getLast(), and list.reversed() gives a reversed view without copying.
items.q: Which Java 21 method gives a reversed view of a List without copying it?
items.a: list.reversed(), from the sequenced collections added in Java 21.

items.title: Hubble's M30, a cluster swimming upstream
items.body: A new Hubble image shows Messier 30, a globular cluster about 27,500 light-years away in Capricornus. Its stars are ancient, some estimated at 11.5 to 13.5 billion years old. M30 orbits against the direction the Milky Way spins, a hint that it may have been born elsewhere and adopted by our galaxy long ago.
items.hook: Wonder: what would the sky look like from inside a ball of a hundred thousand stars?

items.title: Friday, first kettle
items.body:
The kettle clears its throat,
the window learns the colour grey,
a sparrow tests the railing
like it owns the day.
Nothing urgent is awake yet.
I let it stay that way.

items.title: Gemini gets an API for quick decisions
items.body: Google introduced a Gemini Decisions API built for short verdicts rather than long answers. One request can carry up to 1,000 yes/no questions, multiple-choice picks or scoring criteria, and each answer comes back with a confidence score. It accepts text and other media as input.
items.hook: Wonder: how many of your daily tasks are really a long list of small yes/no calls?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Before you scroll, a warm-up: three small questions from this edition are waiting further down. Try answering each before you peek.
items.q: What does 'zugzwang' mean in chess?
items.a: Being forced to move when every move makes your position worse; German for 'compulsion to move'.

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Before you scroll on, try to recall: how old is moonlight? What did 'robota' mean in Czech? Why can a B-tree answer range queries?
items.q: Which comedy show gave Python its name?
items.a: Monty Python's Flying Circus.

items.title: Rehearse the agent before the stage
items.body: Before an agent touches real email or real money, give it a sandbox with fake but realistic data and a few tricky scenarios: a missing file, an ambiguous request, a tool that times out. Watching it handle rehearsals tells you more than any demo, and the fixes are free.

items.title: Pigeons, 7 am
items.body:
They queue on the parapet
like commuters with no train,
puff, shuffle, settle.
One leaves.
The rest move up a step,
as if it were their turn
for the sun.

items.title: Tamarind is a bean
items.body: The tamarind in your rasam comes from a pod, and the tree belongs to the legume family, alongside peas, beans and lentils. The sour pulp surrounds the seeds inside the brown, curved pods.
items.hook: Wonder: which other kitchen staples are secretly legumes?

items.title: Sambuev wins Sahel Chess Festival unbeaten
items.body: Canadian grandmaster Bator Sambuev won the second Sahel Chess Festival in Monastir, Tunisia, with an unbeaten 8/9, ahead of Wafa Hamed and Valerio Carnicelli. More than 300 players took part, and Margarita Potapova earned a WGM norm.
items.q: What score did Sambuev make at the Sahel Chess Festival?
items.a: 8/9, unbeaten.

items.title: Blue-green deployments
items.body: Run two identical environments: blue serves users while green gets the new release. Test green, then switch the router. If something looks off, switch back in seconds. The cost is double capacity during the swap; the gift is a calm, reversible release.
items.hook: Wonder: how fast could you undo your last deployment?

items.title: Sermons in stones
items.body: And this our life, exempt from public haunt, finds tongues in trees, books in the running brooks, sermons in stones, and good in every thing.
items.who: William Shakespeare, As You Like It

items.title: Python is named after a comedy show
items.body: When Guido van Rossum started Python around Christmas 1989, he picked the name because he was reading scripts of Monty Python's Flying Circus and wanted something short and a little mysterious. It was never named after the snake.
items.q: What inspired the name of the Python language?
items.a: Monty Python's Flying Circus.

items.title: Moonlight is about 1.3 seconds old
items.body: The Moon sits roughly 384,000 km away, so light reflected from its surface reaches your eyes in about 1.3 seconds. The moonlight you see is sunlight that has already travelled about eight minutes, bounced, and then taken a short extra hop.
items.q: Roughly how long does light take to travel from the Moon to Earth?
items.a: About 1.3 seconds.

items.title: One 'now' card
items.body: Write the single task you're doing on a sticky note and put it at the edge of your screen. When you surface from a detour, the card answers 'what was I doing?' instantly. Swap the card only when the task is done or deliberately paused.

items.title: Slow the clock when it matters
items.body: Story time doesn't have to match real time. Skip a week in one line, then spend a whole paragraph on the three seconds before a door opens. Readers feel weight where you linger, so linger on the moment that changes things.

items.title: The expertise reversal effect
items.body: Step-by-step guidance that helps beginners can slow experts down: they already hold the steps in their heads, and reading them again adds load. As you improve, swap full worked examples for bare problems. Good teaching fades the scaffolding.
items.q: What is the expertise reversal effect?
items.a: Guidance that helps novices can hinder learners who are already skilled.

items.title: Plurai raises money to build practice worlds for agents
items.body: Plurai announced $13 million in seed funding to build simulation tools where AI agents can be tested and improved before they meet real users. The idea is a flight simulator for agents: rehearse many messy situations safely, then ship.
items.hook: Wonder: what would a 'driving test' for your favourite agent include?

items.title: Rainbows are full circles
items.body: A rainbow is really a circle of light around the point directly opposite the Sun. From the ground the horizon cuts it into an arc, but from an aircraft or a high cliff you can sometimes see the whole ring.
items.q: Why do we usually see only an arc of a rainbow?
items.a: The ground cuts off the lower part of what is really a full circle.

items.title: Ajanta, found again in 1819
items.body: The Buddhist cave temples of Ajanta, carved and painted between roughly the 2nd century BCE and the 5th century CE, slipped out of common memory for centuries. In April 1819 a British officer, John Smith, came upon them from across the ravine and scratched his name on a wall. Today their murals are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
items.hook: Wonder: what kept those paintings safe through centuries of quiet?

items.title: Overloading: one piece, two jobs
items.body: A defender is overloaded when it guards two things at once. Attack one of them and it must choose, leaving the other unguarded. When you spot a piece doing double duty, ask what happens if you make it do just one.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your pieces is quietly holding two posts right now?

items.title: Why indexes are trees
items.body: Most database indexes are B-trees: wide, shallow trees that keep keys in sorted order. Because each node holds hundreds of keys, even a billion rows sit only a few levels deep, so a lookup touches a handful of disk pages. Sorted order is also why the same index serves ranges like 'created between June and July'.
items.q: Why can one B-tree index answer range queries?
items.a: It keeps keys in sorted order, so a range is a contiguous walk.

items.title: ChatGPT opens a front desk for businesses
items.body: OpenAI introduced Businesses in ChatGPT in beta. Verified businesses can claim a profile in a Business Hub, and Business Agents, clearly labelled assistants that speak for a brand, are rolling out first to eligible US online shops and services.
items.q: What is the name of the brand-representing assistants in ChatGPT's new business feature?
items.a: Business Agents.

items.title: The postbox at the corner
items.body: Every evening Mrs. Iyer posted one letter, though no one knew to whom. The postman finally asked. 'To my granddaughter in Pune,' she said. 'She replies by phone, but she keeps the letters in a tin.' The next week the postman left a small note in her own box: 'Your handwriting is the best on my route.' She kept that in a tin too.

items.title: Hubble revisits the Jellyfish Cluster
items.body: New Hubble observations of Messier 30, a globular cluster about 27,500 light-years away in Capricornus, are helping astronomers ask whether some of its ancient stars, or even the whole cluster, first formed outside our galaxy. Its stars are among the oldest in the Milky Way.
items.hook: Wonder: can a star cluster be an immigrant?

items.title: 'Vague but exciting'
items.body: In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee handed his boss at CERN, Mike Sendall, a proposal for an information management system. Sendall wrote 'Vague but exciting...' on the cover and let him carry on. That proposal grew into the World Wide Web.
items.q: What did Mike Sendall write on Tim Berners-Lee's 1989 proposal?
items.a: 'Vague but exciting...'

items.title: Keep learning how to live
items.body: As long as you live, keep learning how to live.

items.title: Lyrics compete with reading
items.body: Research on the 'irrelevant speech effect' finds that background speech, including sung lyrics, makes it harder to hold words in order in memory, even when you try to ignore it. Instrumental music or steady noise interferes far less. For reading and memorising, wordless sound is the kinder choice.
items.hook: Wonder: does your study playlist have words in it?

items.title: Where the word 'robot' came from
items.body: 'Robot' first appeared in Karel Čapek's 1920 Czech play R.U.R. It comes from the Czech robota, meaning forced labour, and Čapek credited his brother Josef with suggesting it.
items.q: Who suggested the word 'robot' to Karel Čapek?
items.a: His brother, Josef Čapek.

items.title: Book the in-between time
items.body: Time blindness often hides in the gaps: the walk, the parking, the 'just finishing this email'. When you add something to your calendar, add a separate 10–15 minute block before it called 'get there'. Transitions stop stealing from the thing itself, and you arrive less rushed.
items.hook: Wonder: how long does getting ready actually take you, start to door?

items.title: Total Chess: four groups, four leaders
items.body: After the first day of Fast Classic group play at the Total Chess pilot in Budapest, Firouzja and Duda lead Group A, Caruana and Liem Le share Group B, Nepomniachtchi leads Group C and Vachier-Lagrave leads Group D, each on 4 points. Carlsen and Giri drew both their games. Wins count 3 points here, so every decisive game matters.
items.hook: Wonder: how does 3 points for a win change the way a top player plays a level position?

items.title: Java: Collectors.partitioningBy
items.q: What keys does partitioningBy always return?
items.a: Both true and false, even when a group is empty.

items.title: Lothal's ancient dock
items.body: At Lothal in Gujarat, Harappan builders around 2400 BCE lined a large rectangular basin with fired bricks. Many archaeologists read it as one of the world's earliest dockyards, linked by channel to a river that led to the sea, with warehouses and bead workshops nearby. Some scholars think it held water instead, which keeps the conversation lively.
items.q: In which present-day Indian state is Lothal?
items.a: Gujarat.

items.title: Gemini Robotics 2.5 steps onto factory floors
items.body: Google DeepMind announced Gemini Robotics 2.5, a model that turns what a robot sees and is told into actions. In reported trials, Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid reached a 96% success rate sorting car parts into kits at Mercedes-Benz plants in Germany and Hungary, and handled obstacles more safely than before.
items.q: Which humanoid robot was reported using Gemini Robotics 2.5 for car-parts kitting?
items.a: Apptronik's Apollo 2.

items.title: Thursday, the fridge hums
items.body:
Everyone asleep.
The fridge keeps its one long note,
the clock adds a soft drum.
I rinse the last cup
and leave it upside down,
ready for morning
like a small promise.

items.title: The oldest close pair of quasars
items.body: Astronomers have found two quasars, brilliantly feeding supermassive black holes, sitting only about 18,100 light-years apart. We see them as they were roughly 900 million years after the Big Bang, and their masses are about 1.5 billion and 400 million Suns. Pairs this close, this early, are a fresh puzzle for how the first giant black holes grew.
items.hook: Wonder: what would the night sky look like from a galaxy with two quasars?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Before you scroll on, try to recall: why does Phobos rise in the west? What does Math.floorMod(-7, 3) return? Which parent seahorse carries the eggs?
items.q: Who is India's 100th grandmaster?
items.a: Anuj Shrivatri.

items.title: Ask for two options, then a pick
items.body: When an agent faces a design choice, ask it to sketch two approaches in a few lines each and then recommend one. You'll see the trade-off it noticed, catch the times its favourite rests on a wrong assumption, and stay the person who decides.
items.hook: Wonder: what did the agent consider and quietly drop last time?

items.title: The Moon has quakes
items.body: Seismometers left by Apollo astronauts recorded moonquakes until 1977. Some are triggered by Earth's tides, some by meteorite impacts, and some by the surface warming and contracting as the long lunar day turns to night. Because the Moon is dry and rigid, it can ring for a long time after a quake.
items.q: How do we know the Moon has quakes?
items.a: Seismometers left by the Apollo missions recorded them until 1977.

items.title: Ledger of things that went right
items.body:
The bus waited.
The dosa was crisp at the edge.
A stranger held a door,
and I held the next one.
Small sums,
but the column is longer than I thought.

items.title: The first letter
items.body: As every letter begins with A, so the whole world begins with the First Being.

items.title: Cursor pagination beats offset
items.body: OFFSET 100000 makes the database walk past a hundred thousand rows before it returns anything, and new rows arriving mid-scroll shift every page. Cursor (or keyset) pagination instead says 'give me 50 rows after id 8812'. It uses the index directly, stays fast on page one thousand, and never shows the same row twice.
items.q: Why does keyset pagination stay fast deep into results?
items.a: It seeks straight to the cursor via the index instead of skipping rows.

items.title: Bishops love pawns on both wings
items.body: When pawns are spread across both sides of the board, a bishop usually beats a knight: it can sweep from one wing to the other in a single move, while the knight needs several hops. With all the pawns on one side, the knight's slowness matters far less.
items.hook: Wonder: in your last endgame, which side were the pawns on?

items.title: COBOL was designed by committee, on purpose
items.body: In 1959 a group called CODASYL, drawing on Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC, designed COBOL so business programs could read almost like English: ADD TAX TO TOTAL. The goal was a language that worked across different manufacturers' machines. Much of it still quietly runs payroll and banking systems today.
items.q: Which earlier language strongly influenced COBOL?
items.a: Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC.

items.title: The Pleiades are up all night
items.body: In November the Pleiades, a little cluster of blue-white stars in Taurus, rise in the east soon after dark and stay up through the night. Most people see six or seven stars by eye. A pair of binoculars turns them into dozens, a sparkling handful of young siblings about 440 light-years away.
items.q: Roughly how many Pleiades stars can most people see without binoculars?
items.a: Six or seven.

items.title: Turn the task into a question
items.body: 'Write the report' is a wall. 'What's the first sentence of the report?' is a door. Rephrasing a task as a small, specific question gives your curiosity something to grab, and once one answer is down the next question usually appears on its own.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the first question hiding inside your biggest task?

items.title: Vikramashila, Nalanda's sister
items.body: Around the end of the 8th century, the Pala king Dharmapala founded Vikramashila in what is now Bihar. It grew into one of the great monastic universities of its age, and its scholar Atisha later travelled to Tibet in the 11th century, where his teaching left a lasting mark.
items.hook: Wonder: what would a reading list at Vikramashila have looked like?

items.title: The tailor's last button
items.body: Every shirt Mr. Ilango finished had one button sewn on with a different thread, a pale blue. Customers rarely noticed. When his granddaughter asked, he said it was so he could find his own work again someday. Forty years later she found a shirt at a secondhand stall in Mylapore, turned the cuff, and there it was: blue, holding.

items.title: The IKEA effect
items.body: In 2012 Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely found people valued items they had assembled themselves, even plain flat-pack boxes, more than identical ones built for them. Effort breeds attachment. It is a useful nudge for learning: notes you make, rather than ones you're handed, tend to feel worth returning to.
items.q: What is the IKEA effect?
items.a: We value things more when we've helped build them.

items.title: Adobe lets outside agents work on real project files
items.body: Adobe added new agent features across Photoshop, Premiere and Firefly, and an MCP integration so outside AI agents can work with editable Adobe project files rather than flattened images. Photoshop 2027 also adds Relight and Generative Restyle.
items.q: What does Adobe's MCP integration let outside agents do?
items.a: Work with editable Adobe project files.

items.title: The cashew grows outside its fruit
items.body: A cashew nut hangs beneath a fleshy, pear-shaped 'cashew apple', in a hard shell of its own. The apple is juicy and eaten fresh in Goa and Brazil, and in Goa it is also used to make feni. The nut has to be roasted or steamed out of its shell, which is why cashews are always sold shelled.
items.hook: Wonder: what does a cashew apple taste like?

items.title: Room for kindness
items.body: Wherever there is a human being, there is an opportunity for a kindness.

items.title: The sidecar pattern
items.body: Instead of building logging, TLS and retries into every service, run a small helper process beside each one: a sidecar. It shares the service's network and lifecycle, so the app talks to localhost and the sidecar handles the plumbing. Service meshes like Istio work this way, and teams can upgrade the plumbing without touching the app.
items.q: What does a sidecar share with the service it sits beside?
items.a: Its network and lifecycle (it starts and stops with it).

items.title: Van Foreest and Martirosyan bounce back in Budapest
items.body: On day two of the Total Chess pilot in Budapest, Jorden van Foreest beat Levon Aronian and Haik Martirosyan beat Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, both recovering from first-round losses. Magnus Carlsen and Anish Giri drew. No one has a perfect score yet, and only the four group winners go through to the title stage.
items.q: How many players from each group reach the Total Chess title stage?
items.a: Only the group winner.

items.title: Let the ending echo the opening
items.body: A short piece feels finished when its last image quietly answers its first. Open on a locked gate, close on someone leaving it open. The reader doesn't need it explained; they feel the circle close, and the change in between becomes the story.
items.hook: Wonder: what object could open and close your next piece?

items.title: The Martian moon that rises in the west
items.body: Phobos, the larger moon of Mars, circles the planet in about 7 hours 39 minutes, faster than Mars turns. So from the Martian surface it rises in the west and sets in the east, crossing the sky roughly twice a day.
items.q: Why does Phobos rise in the west?
items.a: It orbits Mars faster than Mars rotates.

items.title: Keep a 'waiting for' list
items.body: A surprising amount of mental noise comes from things you're waiting on: a reply, a parcel, a form. Give them one short list with the date you asked. Your brain can stop holding them, and a quick weekly glance tells you which ones need a gentle nudge.
items.hook: Wonder: how many open loops are you quietly carrying right now?

items.title: Wi-Fi doesn't stand for anything
items.body: 'Wi-Fi' was coined in 1999 by the branding firm Interbrand as a friendlier name than 'IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence'. It was chosen as a pleasant echo of 'hi-fi'. The phrase 'wireless fidelity' was attached afterwards and was never the real meaning.
items.q: Who coined the name Wi-Fi, and when?
items.a: The branding firm Interbrand, in 1999.

items.title: End every agent run with a changelog
items.body: When an agent finishes, ask it for a short list: files touched, commands run, anything it skipped and why. It takes a few seconds to read, and it turns 'it said it was done' into something you can check. Over time the changelogs also show you which tasks it handles well and which need a closer eye.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you want to know first if a colleague did this work?

items.title: Sanchi's great stupa
items.body: The Great Stupa at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh was first built in the 3rd century BCE under the emperor Ashoka, as a simple brick dome. Later generations enlarged it in stone and added four carved gateways, the toranas, which tell stories from the Buddha's life without ever showing him in human form; he appears as a footprint, a tree or an empty seat.
items.hook: Wonder: how would you tell a story about someone without drawing them?

items.title: Seahorse fathers carry the babies
items.body: In seahorses, the female places her eggs into a pouch on the male's belly. He fertilises them, carries them for a few weeks, and then gives birth to tiny, fully formed seahorses, sometimes hundreds at once.
items.q: Which seahorse parent carries the eggs until birth?
items.a: The father, in a pouch on his belly.

items.title: First and last stick best
items.body: Read someone a list of words and ask them to recall it: the first few and the last few come back most easily, and the middle sags. Psychologists call this the serial position effect, with primacy at the start and recency at the end. If a study session has a middle, give it a quick review on its own.
items.hook: Wonder: which part of today's meeting can you remember least?

items.title: India welcomes its 100th grandmaster
items.body: Anuj Shrivatri, 22, won the ASEAN Plus Open in the Philippines with a performance rating of 2586, completing the requirements for the grandmaster title. He becomes India's 100th GM, a round number that would have been hard to imagine when Viswanathan Anand became the first in 1988.
items.q: Who became India's 100th grandmaster?
items.a: Anuj Shrivatri, aged 22.

items.title: Java: Math.floorMod for wrap-around
items.body: In Java, -7 % 3 is -1, because % keeps the sign of the left side. That surprises anyone wrapping an index around a ring buffer or a clock face. Math.floorMod(-7, 3) returns 2, which is usually what you meant: a result that is never negative when the divisor is positive.
items.q: What does Math.floorMod(-7, 3) return?
items.a: 2 (whereas -7 % 3 is -1).

items.title: ElevenLabs releases Scribe v3
items.body: ElevenLabs has a new speech-to-text model, Scribe v3, plus a live version for real-time use. In its multilingual tests the company reports about 27% fewer word errors than Scribe v2, and the live version adds speaker labels so a transcript knows who said what.
items.q: What does Scribe v3 Live add for conversations?
items.a: Speaker diarization: labels for who said what.

items.title: Thursday, before the milk comes
items.body:
The street is still deciding
what colour it will be.
A crow tries one word, then another.
I hold the tumbler with both hands,
not because it is cold,
but because the morning is.
items.hook: Wonder: what small object anchors your first ten minutes?

items.title: The planet that stopped crossing its star
items.body: Astronomers following the hot Jupiter TOI-2535 b with NASA's TESS satellite from 2019 to 2026 watched its transits drift early and late by up to six hours, grow shorter and shallower, and then stop altogether. A hidden neighbour on a tilted orbit is slowly tipping its path, so for now it simply misses our line of sight. The team expects it to start transiting again in 30 to 50 years.
items.q: Why did TOI-2535 b stop transiting?
items.a: A neighbouring planet on a tilted orbit is slowly tipping its orbit out of our line of sight.

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Before you scroll on, try to recall: what does Voyager's Morse message spell? Which piece did Nimzowitsch prefer as a blockader? What is the dot on an i called?
items.q: What did Carlsen score in the Budapest opening blitz?
items.a: 7/9, unbeaten.

items.title: Before sleep
items.body:
The fan counts the same four words.
A neighbour's tap runs, stops.
I set down the day
the way you set down a full glass,
slowly, watching the rim,
and nothing spills.

items.title: WikiTrace: agent memory you can trace back
items.body: Researchers describe WikiTrace, a memory design for agents with three linked layers: short lessons, compiled summaries, and the raw records of past runs they came from. Across five agent benchmarks it averaged 90.2%, versus 87.0% with lessons alone and 79.5% with no memory, while adding only about 17% extra compute at test time.
items.q: What three layers does WikiTrace link?
items.a: Insights (lessons), compilations, and the raw run trajectories.

items.title: A jiffy is a real unit
items.body: 'Back in a jiffy' sounds vague, but scientists have borrowed the word for exact durations. In physics it has been used for the time light takes to cross one centimetre, about 33 trillionths of a second. In computing, a jiffy is one tick of the system timer. Either way, it's quicker than anyone who says it.

items.title: Change data capture: read the database's diary
items.body: Every serious database keeps a log of its changes for its own recovery. Change data capture tools such as Debezium read that log and publish each insert, update and delete as an event. Search indexes, caches and analytics can follow along without the application having to remember to tell them, and without polling.
items.hook: Wonder: what other systems already keep a diary you could read?

items.title: Your own friend
items.body: Lift yourself by your own effort; do not let yourself sink. You alone can be your own best friend.

items.title: Blockade the passed pawn
items.body: Aron Nimzowitsch, born 140 years ago this month, taught that a passed pawn should be stopped by a piece placed directly in front of it. A knight is ideal: it isn't hemmed in by the pawn, and from that square it still reaches in every direction. 'First restrain, then blockade, then destroy' is the order he recommended.
items.q: Which piece did Nimzowitsch consider the best blockader?
items.a: The knight.

items.title: The first text message said 'Merry Christmas'
items.body: On 3 December 1992, engineer Neil Papworth sent 'Merry Christmas' from a computer to a mobile phone on the Vodafone network in the UK. Phones couldn't yet type replies, so the recipient simply read it. Within a decade, texting had become one of the most common ways people talk.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you send if you knew it was the first message ever?

items.title: Mars and Jupiter meet before dawn on 15 November
items.body: Mars and Jupiter will be at their closest around 3 UTC on 15 November (8:30 am IST, so look in the hours before sunrise, low in the east). Mars passes about 1.2 degrees north of Jupiter, a little more than two full-Moon widths. Jupiter will be the brighter of the two; Mars has a faint orange tint.
items.q: Which is brighter in the 15 November pairing, Mars or Jupiter?
items.a: Jupiter.

items.title: Keep a few ready-made replies
items.body: Small replies stall because each one needs a fresh start: 'Thanks, received', 'Can we move this to Thursday?', 'Here's the file you asked for'. Save your five most common messages as text shortcuts or notes. Sending one becomes a tap and a tweak, not a blank screen.

items.title: Music written on a rock at Kudumiyanmalai
items.body: On a rock face at Kudumiyanmalai, in Tamil Nadu's Pudukkottai district, there is an inscription from around the 7th century that records musical notation. It is one of the oldest surviving written records of Indian music, and it is often linked to the Pallava king Mahendravarman I, though scholars still discuss the attribution.
items.q: Where is the old rock inscription recording musical notation?
items.a: Kudumiyanmalai, in Pudukkottai district, Tamil Nadu.

items.title: Let the reader arrive a beat early
items.body: If the reader can guess what a character is about to realise, just a moment before the character does, they lean in. Plant one small clue earlier in the scene, then let the character catch up. The reader feels clever, not tricked, and the realisation lands twice: once in them, once on the page.

items.title: Anthropic adds Sheets, Meetings and Whiteboards to Claude
items.body: At an event in San Francisco on 10 November, Anthropic introduced Claude Sheets (in beta on paid plans, with Excel export), Claude Meetings, which can join Google Meet calls for Team and Enterprise users, and Claude Whiteboards. Claude Data, the renamed Dashboards, became generally available alongside plugins for Adobe, Atlassian and HubSpot.

items.title: Avocados ripen only after picking
items.body: An avocado stays firm while it hangs on the tree; it only begins to soften after it's picked. Growers can leave fruit on the branch for weeks or months as a kind of living storage. At home, putting one in a paper bag with a banana speeds things up, thanks to the ripening gas ethylene.
items.hook: Wonder: what else in your kitchen is quietly waiting for its cue?

items.title: Name the feeling
items.body: In a 2007 study led by Matthew Lieberman, people who picked a word for the emotion in a photo showed less amygdala activity than people who simply looked at it or matched it to another face. Researchers call this affect labelling. Quietly naming what you feel ('this is frustration') can take a little of the heat out of it.
items.q: What is affect labelling?
items.a: Putting a feeling into words, which in studies dampened emotional reactivity.

items.title: Java: a default without the ternary
items.body: Instead of `name != null ? name : "guest"`, write `Objects.requireNonNullElse(name, "guest")` (Java 9+). If the default is expensive to build, use `requireNonNullElseGet(name, () -> loadDefault())` so it's only created when needed. Small, but the intent reads in one glance.
items.q: Which method avoids building an expensive default unless it's needed?
items.a: Objects.requireNonNullElseGet, with a Supplier.

items.title: Vaishali beats Niemann and So in Budapest
items.body: In the Total Chess opening blitz, R. Vaishali beat Hans Niemann in round 1 and Wesley So in round 3, both with Black, and drew with Duda, Rapport, Giri and Assaubayeva, finishing on 4/9. She now plays in Group D alongside So, Arjun Erigaisi, Vachier-Lagrave, Niemann and Assaubayeva.

items.title: The bell at the cycle shop
items.body: Murugan's cycle shop had a bell on the door that had lost its clapper years ago. Customers still pushed the door and paused, waiting for the ring that never came. Murugan liked that pause. It was the moment people stopped hurrying. One evening a boy fixed the bell with a bolt from the spare-parts tin and rang it proudly. Murugan thanked him, and that night he took the bolt out again, gently, and kept it in his shirt pocket as a gift.
items.hook: Wonder: what small 'broken' thing in your day actually helps you slow down?

items.title: Wave at Voyager 1 in Morse code
items.body: NASA says Voyager 1 will be one light-day from Earth at 10:16 UTC on 18 November 2026 (3:46 pm IST), about 25.9 billion kilometres away, 49 years after launch. To mark it, NASA's 'Shine Bright' event invites people to flash V-G-R in Morse code with a torch after sunset on 17 November: dot-dot-dot-dash, dash-dash-dot, dot-dash-dot.
