items.hook: Wonder: a message from Earth now takes a whole day to reach it. What would you send?

items.title: Moore's law began as a 1965 magazine piece
items.body: In 1965 Gordon Moore wrote an article for Electronics magazine predicting that the number of components on a chip would double about every year. In 1975 he revised the pace to roughly every two years. It was an observation about engineering and economics, not a law of physics, yet the industry treated it as a target for decades.
items.q: How did Moore revise his prediction in 1975?
items.a: From doubling about every year to roughly every two years.

items.title: Smile at it
items.body: When trouble comes, meet it with a smile; nothing overcomes trouble quite like that.

items.title: Reminders that know where you are
items.body: Time-based reminders often fire when you can't act on them. Most phones can remind you by place instead: 'buy batteries' when you reach the shop, 'take the parcel' when you leave home. The nudge arrives at the one moment it's useful, so you don't have to hold it in mind all day.

items.title: Give the agent a way to say 'blocked'
items.body: Agents tend to keep trying when they hit a wall: a missing permission, a vague requirement, a test that can't run. Add an explicit 'blocked' outcome with a short reason, and make it a respectable result rather than a failure. You'll get fewer creative workarounds and a clearer picture of what actually needs a human.

items.title: Aathichoodi: Tamil wisdom in alphabetical order
items.body: Avvaiyar's Aathichoodi is a set of very short lines of advice, each beginning with the next letter of the Tamil alphabet. The first, 'Aram seya virumbu', means 'Love to do good'. Because each line is only a few words and follows the alphabet, generations of Tamil children have learned their letters and their values together.
items.hook: Wonder: what would your own alphabet of one-line advice say?

items.title: The dot on the i has a name
items.body: The little dot above a lowercase i or j is called a tittle. The word is centuries old, and it may even be behind the phrase 'to a T', meaning exactly, though that origin isn't certain.
items.q: What is the dot above a lowercase i called?
items.a: A tittle.

items.title: Rendezvous hashing: let every node bid
items.body: To decide which server owns a key, compute a score for every server, hash(key + server), and pick the highest. That's rendezvous (highest-random-weight) hashing. If a server leaves, only its keys move, each to its next-highest bidder; everything else stays put. It needs no ring and no virtual nodes, at the cost of scoring every server per lookup.
items.q: In rendezvous hashing, which server owns a key?
items.a: The one with the highest hash(key, server) score.

items.title: Write it down to think better
items.body: Working memory holds only a few things at a time. Psychologists call it cognitive offloading when you move some of that load into the world: a note, a sketch, a list. Research reviewed by Evan Risko and Sam Gilbert suggests people offload naturally when a task gets heavy, and it often improves performance. A messy scratch page is not a sign of weakness; it's extra working memory.
items.hook: Wonder: which part of today's work could live on paper instead of in your head?

items.title: Carlsen wins the Total Chess opening blitz unbeaten
items.body: The Total Chess pilot in Budapest began on 10 November with a nine-round blitz Swiss for 24 players. Magnus Carlsen finished on 7/9 with five wins and four draws, half a point ahead of Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, with Levon Aronian third on 6. The blitz doesn't award prize money; it sets tiebreaks for the group stage, which runs 11 to 15 November at 45 minutes plus 30 seconds a move.
items.q: What was Carlsen's score in the Budapest opening blitz?
items.a: 7/9, unbeaten (five wins, four draws).

items.title: A lava world wearing a reflective veil
items.body: Webb watched the super-Earth TOI-561 b for 37 hours, covering three of its orbits; it circles its star in under 10.5 hours, about 280 light-years away in Sextans. A planet that close should be scorched bare, yet the light suggests reflective clouds or haze that bounce much of the starlight back into space, like a sunscreen.
items.q: How long does TOI-561 b take to orbit its star?
items.a: Under 10.5 hours.

items.title: Wednesday, lamps on
items.body:
The vegetable cart folds its last shade.
A boy carries home a single bulb
as if it might spill.
Windows take their turns lighting up,
slow and unhurried,
like someone counting
who doesn't mind losing their place.

items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon reaches the paid API
items.body: Google has made Gemini 4 Carbon available to paid API and AI Ultra users, at an introductory $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until 30 November. Google says it ranks first on several agent benchmarks, including CursorBench 4.0. It also brings a /swarm feature to Antigravity that turns a single prompt into a small team of coordinated agents.
items.hook: Wonder: when one prompt becomes a team, who decides which agent does what?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Before you scroll on, try to recall: what kind of engine is NASA's AMPERE prize for? Which way do grown-up sunflowers face? Which Chola temple is carved as a chariot?
items.q: Why does a solar day on Mercury last two of its years?
items.a: It spins slowly (59 days) while orbiting in 88 days, so sunrise to sunrise takes about 176 Earth days.

items.title: Terrace, after the rain
items.body:
Water stands in the dent of the old chair.
The neem shakes off what it was holding.
Somewhere a radio finds its station,
loses it, finds it again.
I do the same with the evening.

items.title: The kiwi's very big egg
items.body: A female kiwi lays an egg that can be around a fifth of her own body weight, one of the largest eggs relative to body size of any bird. The chick hatches well developed, with a yolk store that keeps it going for its first days.

items.title: Read the trace, not just the answer
items.body: An agent's final answer tells you what it concluded; its trace tells you how. When something goes wrong, the steps (which files it read, which tool calls failed, where it guessed) usually show the real fix faster than rewriting the prompt. Make the trace easy to read, and you'll improve the agent faster.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you learn if you watched every step of your own work as closely?

items.title: Like a good book
items.body: The company of the good is like a fine book: the more often you return to it, the more it gives.

items.title: Java: groupingBy in one line
items.body: Collectors.groupingBy turns a list into a map of lists. For example, orders.stream().collect(groupingBy(Order::city)) gives a Map from each city to its orders. Add a second collector to summarise each group: groupingBy(Order::city, counting()) gives a count per city instead of the full lists.

items.title: A rook on the seventh rank
items.body: A rook that reaches the opponent's second rank (your seventh) is often worth an extra pawn's activity. From there it attacks pawns that haven't moved and can trap the enemy king on its back rank. Two rooks doubled on the seventh are strong enough that players have a nickname for them: 'pigs on the seventh', because they eat everything.
items.q: Why is a rook on the seventh rank so strong?
items.a: It attacks unmoved pawns and can confine the enemy king to its back rank.

items.title: TIFRAC, an early computer built in India
items.body: TIFRAC (Tata Institute of Fundamental Research Automatic Calculator) was designed and built at TIFR in Bombay in the late 1950s and was in use by 1960. It was one of the first electronic digital computers built in India, using thousands of vacuum tubes and a ferrite-core memory. It served Indian scientists for several years before commercial machines took over.
items.hook: Wonder: what does it take to build a computer when there is no one to buy one from?

items.title: Give messages their own visiting hours
items.body: Turn off most notifications and pick two or three set times a day to check messages. Write those times on a sticky note so your brain can trust they'll come. Batching messages turns a hundred small interruptions into a few short, finished visits.

items.title: The Orion Nebula is a nursery you can see
items.body: On November nights Orion climbs into the eastern sky by late evening. Below his belt hangs a short line of stars, his sword, and the fuzzy middle 'star' is the Orion Nebula, a cloud where new stars are forming about 1,300 light-years away. Even ordinary binoculars show it as a soft glow.
items.q: What is the fuzzy patch in Orion's sword?
items.a: The Orion Nebula, a star-forming cloud about 1,300 light-years away.

items.title: Open with a question the reader wants answered
items.body: A first line works when it makes the reader curious about something specific. 'The letter had been posted in 1994 and arrived on a Tuesday' asks a question without saying so. You don't need a mystery, just one small gap the reader wants filled, and then the patience to fill it at the right moment.

items.title: Tip-of-the-tongue moments are normal
items.body: Most people have a word stuck on the tip of the tongue now and then, often for names. You frequently know the first letter or the number of syllables while the word itself hides. Usually it turns up on its own a little later, so it helps to note what you were reaching for and move on.
items.hook: Wonder: how can you know a word's first letter without knowing the word?

items.title: Korkai, the pearl port of the Pandyas
items.body: Korkai, near the mouth of the Tamirabarani river, was an early port of the Pandya kings and was known for its pearl fishery. Greek and Roman writers knew it too: the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea and Ptolemy mention a pearl-fishing place called Kolchoi. Over centuries the shoreline moved, and Korkai now sits a few kilometres inland.
items.q: What was the ancient Pandya port of Korkai famous for?
items.a: Its pearl fishery.

items.title: Anthropic releases Claude Fable 5.2
items.body: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, aimed at long, complex technical work. Fable is available to everyone, while Mythos, which keeps some specialist capabilities, is offered to verified organisations. Anthropic says a team of more than 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents worked together for eight days to build a bootable operating system; that's the company's own report.

items.title: The platypus glows
items.body: Under ultraviolet light, platypus fur gives off a soft blue-green glow. Researchers reported it in 2020 after checking museum specimens. Nobody is yet sure whether the glow does anything for the animal or is simply a quirk of its fur.

items.title: Load shedding: say no early, and politely
items.body: When a service gets more requests than it can handle, trying to serve all of them can make it slow for everyone. Load shedding means refusing some work early, often with a quick 'try again later' (HTTP 503), so the requests you do accept still finish quickly. Good systems shed the least important work first, like background jobs before checkout.
items.hook: Wonder: when is 'not now' the most helpful answer a server can give?

items.title: Tata Steel 2027 announces its fields
items.body: The 89th Tata Steel Chess tournament will run from 15 to 31 January 2027 in Wijk aan Zee, Netherlands. Defending champion Nodirbek Abdusattorov leads a 14-player Masters field that includes Javokhir Sindarov, Levon Aronian, Anish Giri, Alireza Firouzja and India's Nihal Sarin. India's Aravindh Chithambaram plays in the Challengers.
items.q: Where is the Tata Steel Chess tournament held?
items.a: Wijk aan Zee, Netherlands.

items.title: The lamp repairer
items.body: Every lamp that came to Selvi's stall arrived with a story. 'It flickers when it rains,' said one man. 'It was my mother's,' said a girl, holding it like a bird. Selvi never asked more than she needed. She rewired, she polished, she tested each one in the dim corner by the cloth shop. On Sundays she kept one lamp lit that nobody had ever come back for. It was the brightest on the street, and she liked to think it was waiting patiently, the way she did.

items.title: Mercury's long, slow day
items.body: Mercury circles the Sun in 88 Earth days and spins once every 59 days. Put together, one sunrise to the next takes about 176 Earth days, so a single solar day on Mercury lasts two of its years.
items.hook: Wonder: what would a calendar look like if one day lasted two years?

items.title: Ctrl+Alt+Del was a developer's shortcut
items.body: David Bradley, an engineer on the original IBM PC in 1981, created the Ctrl+Alt+Del key combination so developers could restart a machine without switching it off. He picked keys far apart on purpose, so nobody would press all three by accident. It was never meant for everyday users, which is why it feels a little awkward.
items.q: Why were Ctrl, Alt and Del chosen for the restart shortcut?
items.a: They were far apart, so it was hard to press them all by accident.

items.title: Few things
items.body: Occupy thyself with few things, says the philosopher, if thou wouldst be tranquil.

items.title: Wakeful rest: let it settle
items.body: In studies by Michaela Dewar and colleagues, people who sat quietly for about ten minutes after learning a list remembered more later than people who went straight on to another task. The quiet seems to give fresh memories a chance to settle before new information crowds in. After a hard study block, try a few minutes of doing nothing at all, no phone.
items.q: What did Dewar's studies find about resting quietly right after learning?
items.a: A few minutes of quiet rest improved later recall compared with starting a new task.

items.title: Meta's smallest Muse model, built for repetitive agent work
items.body: Meta has released Muse Ember, the smallest and most efficient model in its Muse family. It is aimed at the many small, repeated steps agents take, rather than at deep reasoning, and is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens through Meta's Model API. Small, cheap models doing the routine steps, with bigger ones called only when needed, is becoming a common agent design.
items.hook: Wonder: how much of an agent's day is routine work that a small model could do?

items.title: Darasuram's temple on wheels
items.body: The Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram, near Kumbakonam, was built by the Chola king Rajaraja II in the 12th century. Its front hall is carved as a chariot, complete with stone wheels and horses. Together with Thanjavur and Gangaikonda Cholapuram it forms the UNESCO World Heritage site called the Great Living Chola Temples.
items.q: Which Chola king built the Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram?
items.a: Rajaraja II, in the 12th century.

items.title: Two choices, not ten
items.body: When a decision stalls you (what to eat, which task first), shrink the menu to two options and pick one within a minute. A short list keeps the decision from swallowing the energy meant for the task. Any reasonable pick, made quickly, usually beats the perfect pick made an hour later.

items.title: Java: strip() knows more spaces than trim()
items.body: String.trim() removes characters up to U+0020, which covers the ASCII space and control characters. Java 11's strip() uses Character.isWhitespace, so it also removes Unicode whitespace such as the ideographic space. For text that arrives from users in many languages, strip(), stripLeading() and stripTrailing() are usually the kinder choice.
items.q: Which Java method removes Unicode whitespace: trim() or strip()?
items.a: strip() (Java 11+). trim() only handles characters up to U+0020.

items.title: Grown-up sunflowers face east
items.body: Young sunflowers really do follow the Sun, turning west by day and back east overnight. Once they open, most stop and settle facing east. A 2016 study found that east-facing heads warm up faster in the morning and draw more bee visits.
items.hook: Wonder: what does a flower gain by greeting the morning?

items.title: Movahed takes his fourth Titled Tuesday of the year
items.body: GM Sina Movahed won the 10 November Titled Tuesday on 9.5 points, edging GM Denis Lazavik on tiebreak, with GM Dmitry Andreikin third on 9. It was Movahed's fourth Titled Tuesday win of 2026, level with Jan-Krzysztof Duda for the most this year. He recovered from a fifth-round loss to Christopher Yoo to finish on top.
items.q: Who finished second to Sina Movahed on tiebreak?
items.a: GM Denis Lazavik, also on 9.5.

items.title: Wednesday, first light
items.body:
The milk packet waits on the step,
cold as a small moon.
A crow tests the parapet,
thinks better of it.
Inside, the kettle starts its long vowel,
and the day, not yet asked for anything,
sits down beside me.

items.title: NASA offers a prize for gentler, longer-lasting thrusters
items.body: NASA has opened the AMPERE Challenge, a $500,000 competition for US companies to build working Hall-effect thrusters in the 3 to 7 kilowatt range. These engines push charged particles with electric and magnetic fields: the thrust is tiny, but they sip propellant, which suits patient jobs like nudging a satellite's orbit over months. Registration runs until 27 January 2027.
items.hook: Wonder: why would a spacecraft prefer a whisper of thrust that lasts for months over one big push?

items.title: IBM and Microsoft team up on 'Imagine Enterprise'
items.body: On 10 November IBM and Microsoft announced Imagine Enterprise, a platform for building, running and governing AI agents that carry out industry-specific work. IBM brings more than 6,000 prebuilt agents and assets from its consulting arm; Microsoft supplies the cloud, data and security layer. The first ready-made frameworks cover financial services, insurance and retail.
items.q: How many prebuilt agents and assets does IBM Consulting bring to Imagine Enterprise?
items.a: More than 6,000.

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Before you scroll on, try to recall: what made the Cat's Tail near Beta Pictoris? What does a bulkhead protect a service from? Who built a calculator for his tax-official father?
items.q: Who built the Pascaline, and for whom?
items.a: Blaise Pascal, around 1642, to help his father with tax sums.

items.title: Evening, the last bus
items.body:
The conductor counts his coins
into little towers by the window.
Nobody is in a hurry now.
The road hums, the jasmine on the dashboard
nods at every turn,
and the town, one lit door at a time,
goes home.

items.title: Stripe's internal helper agent, built in about a week
items.body: Stripe described Kai, a company-wide productivity agent built in roughly a week on LangChain's LangGraph and Deep Agents tools. It reportedly reached around 5,000 internal users within about a month. The appeal of small, quick internal agents is that they meet people where their daily work already happens.
items.q: Roughly how long did it take Stripe to build its internal agent Kai?
items.a: About a week.

items.title: The turtle that breathes through its tail end
items.body: Australia's Fitzroy River turtle can take up oxygen through its cloaca, the opening at the back of its body, drawing in water across thin, blood-rich surfaces. This lets it stay underwater for very long stretches without coming up for air.
items.hook: Wonder: how many other ways of breathing has evolution tried?

items.title: Optimistic locking: check the version, then write
items.body: Instead of locking a row while a user edits it, keep a version number. Read the row with its version, and when saving, update only if the version is still the same, bumping it as you go. If someone else saved first, nothing changes and you retry with fresh data. It works beautifully when conflicts are rare.
items.q: In optimistic locking, what tells you someone else saved first?
items.a: The version number no longer matches, so the update affects zero rows.

items.title: A staff on slippery ground
items.body: The words of good people are like a walking stick on slippery ground: they keep you on your feet.

items.title: The coffee pot that went online
items.body: In 1991, people in the Cambridge University Computer Lab got tired of walking to the Trojan Room coffee pot and finding it empty. They pointed a camera at it and wrote a small program to show the image on their screens. In 1993 it went on the web, and it's often called the first webcam.
items.q: What did the famous Trojan Room camera watch?
items.a: A coffee pot in the Cambridge Computer Lab.

items.title: Interference: when similar things blur
items.body: Learning two very similar things back to back can make them blur: the new phone number trips over the old one. Psychologists call this interference. A gentle fix is to study similar items side by side on purpose and name the difference out loud, so each one gets its own handle.
items.hook: Wonder: which two things do you keep mixing up, and what's the one difference between them?

items.title: Give each scene one clear change
items.body: Before writing a scene, finish this sentence: at the start ___, by the end ___. A secret is out, a door closes, a mind turns. If nothing is different by the end, the scene may belong inside another one. Small changes are fine; they just have to be real.
items.q: What quick test tells you if a scene earns its place?
items.a: Something is different at the end than at the start.

items.title: Tal, the magician, was born 90 years ago
items.body: Mikhail Tal was born in Riga on 9 November 1936. Known as the Magician from Riga, he played wild, sacrificial attacks that were often hard to refute over the board, and he won the world title in 1960 at 23. His lesson for the rest of us: sometimes asking the opponent difficult questions is worth a pawn or two.
items.hook: Wonder: when did you last make a move just to ask a hard question?

items.title: Stones that ring
items.body: At the Vittala temple in Hampi, built in the Vijayanagara era, the slender stone pillars of the main hall are known as musical pillars: tapped gently, different columns give different tones. Visitors today are asked not to tap them, so the stones stay whole for the next few centuries.
items.q: Which Hampi temple is famous for its musical pillars?
items.a: The Vittala temple.

items.title: Pair the dull with the pleasant
items.body: Save something you enjoy for a task you avoid: a favourite podcast only while folding laundry, a nice tea only during email. Researchers call this temptation bundling. The dull task borrows a little of the pleasant one's pull, and you get to stop waiting for motivation.
items.hook: Wonder: which small treat could you link to tomorrow's least favourite chore?

items.title: The Saturn V's first flight
items.body: On 9 November 1967, the Saturn V flew for the first time on Apollo 4, with no crew aboard. It tested all three stages at once, restarted the third stage in orbit, and sent the command module back into the atmosphere at Moon-return speed to prove its heat shield. Just over a year later, Saturn V carried people around the Moon.
items.q: Was anyone aboard Apollo 4?
items.a: No, it was an uncrewed test of the Saturn V.

items.title: Tell the agent what 'done' looks like
items.body: Agents tend to either stop too early or keep polishing forever. Give them a finish line they can check: 'done when the tests pass and the README mentions the new flag'. A concrete stop condition saves time, tokens and second-guessing on both sides.
items.hook: Wonder: could you write the finish line of today's task in one sentence?

items.title: Java: EnumMap when the keys are an enum
items.body: If your map's keys are an enum, use EnumMap. Internally it's a plain array indexed by each constant's ordinal, so it's compact and fast, and it iterates in the enum's declared order. new EnumMap<>(Day.class) is all it takes.
items.q: In what order does an EnumMap iterate its keys?
items.a: In the order the enum constants are declared.

items.title: The clockmaker's quiet hour
items.body: Every shop clock in the lane ran a little wrong, and everyone knew to ask Mr. Rao for the real time. At four each afternoon he wound them all, one after another, and for a moment the whole street seemed to tick together. He never set them exactly right. 'If they all agreed,' he said, 'nobody would come in to ask.'

items.title: Yu Yangyi keeps his Chinese Rapid title
items.body: In Shaoxing, GM Yu Yangyi retained the Chinese Rapid Championship, beating 18-year-old Xiao Tong in a final that was level after rapid and blitz games and went to an Armageddon decider, which Yu won on move 48. Xiao had knocked out Ding Liren earlier. Lu Shanglei finished third.
items.q: How was the Chinese Rapid final finally decided?
items.a: By an Armageddon game, won by Yu Yangyi.

items.title: Why honey keeps
items.body: Sealed honey resists spoiling for a very long time. It holds very little water, it's mildly acidic, and an enzyme bees add slowly produces a little hydrogen peroxide. Microbes that land in it get the water pulled right out of them. If it crystallises, it hasn't gone bad; warm the jar gently and it turns clear again.
items.q: Does crystallised honey mean it has spoiled?
items.a: No. It's just sugar forming crystals; gentle warming reverses it.

items.title: Pascal's adding machine
items.body: Around 1642, a teenage Blaise Pascal built a mechanical calculator to help his father, a tax official in Rouen, with endless sums. Turning dials moved geared wheels, and a clever ratchet carried a one to the next wheel, just like carrying in long addition. He made around fifty of these 'Pascalines' over the following decade.
items.hook: Wonder: how do you make a gear 'carry the one'?

items.title: The quiet room inside
items.body: Nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul.

items.title: NASA's step-by-step road back to the Moon
items.body: NASA has laid out a two-step plan. Artemis III, in 2027, is a crewed test flight in Earth orbit, where four astronauts on Orion will practise meeting and docking with the Blue Moon and Starship landers. Artemis IV, planned for 2028, is the landing itself. NASA also says rocket preparation times have been cut by about half.
items.q: What is Artemis III now planned to practise?
items.a: Rendezvous and docking with the lunar landers, in Earth orbit, in 2027.

items.title: The forgetting curve
items.body: In 1885 Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself over days. Forgetting was steep at first and then levelled off. The kind part: each review made the next drop gentler. A short look back a day later, then a few days later, saves far more than one long session.
items.q: What did Ebbinghaus find about forgetting over time?
items.a: It's fastest at first, then levels off, and each review slows it further.

items.title: Same model, different harness, very different results
items.body: A researcher compared nine coding-agent harnesses running the same open models across nearly 29,000 trials. The harness alone moved the solve rate by about two times and the cost per solved task by roughly ten times or more. One updated harness jumped from near the bottom to tied for first. The quiet lesson: the scaffolding around a model matters as much as the model.
items.hook: Wonder: how much of 'the model is smart' is really 'the loop around it is well built'?

items.title: Madhava's infinite series
items.body: Madhava of Sangamagrama, who lived in Kerala around 1340 to 1425, founded a school of mathematics and astronomy. He and his students worked out infinite series for pi, sine and cosine, ideas that appeared in Europe only about two to three centuries later with Gregory, Newton and Leibniz. Much of his work survives through later Kerala texts such as the Yuktibhasa, written in Malayalam.
items.q: Which region was home to Madhava's school of mathematics?
items.a: Kerala (Sangamagrama, near present-day Irinjalakuda).

items.title: The two-minute version
items.body: When a task feels too big to begin, ask: what's the two-minute version? Not 'clean the kitchen' but 'put the cups in the sink'. Not 'write the report' but 'type the three headings'. Starting is often the hardest part; once you're moving, you're free to stop or keep going. Both count.
items.q: What question helps shrink a task you can't start?
items.a: What's the two-minute version of this?

items.title: Bulkheads: one leak shouldn't sink the ship
items.body: Ships are split into watertight compartments so one hole floods one room, not the whole hull. Services can do the same: give each downstream dependency its own small thread pool or connection pool. If the recommendations service gets slow, it can only tie up its own ten threads, and checkout keeps working with the rest.
items.hook: Wonder: which one slow dependency in your system could currently use up every thread?

items.title: Pranesh wins the first Chola Chess Open
items.body: GM Pranesh M won the inaugural Chola Chess Open in Chennai with 7/9, half a point clear, after beating Iniyan Panneerselvam in the final round. S. L. Narayanan took second on tiebreak. The event produced nine title norms, including a second GM norm for 16-year-old Viresh Sharnarthi and a first IM norm for 11-year-old Sarbartho Mani.
items.q: How many title norms came out of the first Chola Chess Open?
items.a: Nine.

items.title: Night train, Tuesday
items.body:
The carriage lights go soft at ten.
A child asleep on a folded shawl,
a man peeling an orange in one long ribbon,
the window showing only us.
Outside, somewhere, a village
with one lamp on,
keeping the dark company.

items.title: A 93-billion-mile tail of dust around a young star
items.body: Hubble has taken the first visible-light pictures of the 'Cat's Tail', a long, dark streak of dust beside the young star Beta Pictoris, about 63 light-years away. The structure stretches roughly 93 billion miles. Researchers think it is debris from a collision between two Pluto-sized bodies, made of very porous, carbon-rich grains about a micron across.
items.q: What do astronomers think made the 'Cat's Tail' near Beta Pictoris?
items.a: A collision between two Pluto-sized bodies; the tail is the leftover dust.

items.title: DeepMind's agents check Signal's crypto code, proof by proof
items.body: Google DeepMind introduced AlphaProof Code, a team of cooperating AI agents that write formal proofs in the Lean language. In about four weeks they verified the core cryptographic code of the Signal protocol all the way down to machine instructions, flagging roughly 1% of the code for people to review by hand. As a test, the team slipped two old, already-fixed bugs back into a copy, and the system produced checked proofs that those versions were unsafe.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you trust more, a test that passed or a proof that can't be wrong?

items.title: Bus depot, 8 pm
items.body:
Engines settle like tired cattle.
A conductor counts coins into a cloth bag,
the same small music every night.
The last bus sighs its doors shut.
Above the tin roof, one star
clocks in for its shift.

items.title: Write the spec, then the code
items.body: An agent that starts typing code straight away bakes its guesses into the design. A short written spec first, covering what is being built, what it won't do and how you'll know it works, gives you a cheap moment to catch a misunderstanding. Editing two paragraphs is much easier than unwinding two hundred lines.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the smallest spec that would have saved your last rework?

items.title: Sticky sessions vs stateless servers
items.body: A load balancer can send each user back to the same server ('sticky sessions'), which is simple when that server holds the user's session in memory. But it makes scaling and restarts awkward: lose the server and you lose the session. The calmer design is to keep servers stateless and put session data in a shared store like Redis, so any server can answer any request.
items.q: Why do stateless servers make scaling easier?
items.a: Any server can handle any request, so you can add, remove or restart servers without losing user sessions.

items.title: To thine own self
items.body:
This above all: to thine own self be true,
And it must follow, as the night the day,
Thou canst not then be false to any man.

items.title: Sloths are patient swimmers
items.body: Sloths move slowly on land, but they swim well, using a breaststroke-like motion. By slowing their heart rate, they can hold their breath for up to about 40 minutes, longer than many marine mammals.
items.hook: Wonder: what else looks slow only because we watch it in the wrong place?

items.title: Nakamura wins a come-from-behind Bullet Brawl
items.body: Hikaru Nakamura won Chess.com's 7 November Bullet Brawl, a two-hour one-minute arena with 225 players, finishing on 165 points. Ediz Gurel led for much of the event, but Nakamura closed it with a run of six straight wins to finish 12 points ahead. Parham Maghsoodloo was third.

items.title: The transistor's quiet debut
items.body: In December 1947, at Bell Labs, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, working in William Shockley's group, got a small point-contact device to amplify a signal. It was the first working transistor. The three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics, and every chip today carries billions of the transistor's descendants.
items.q: Where and when was the first working transistor demonstrated?
items.a: Bell Labs, December 1947.

items.title: Decide your 'stuck' move in advance
items.body: Getting stuck isn't a failure; staying stuck for an hour is just expensive. Before you start, pick your stuck move: after ten minutes with no progress, I'll write down the exact question, ask someone, or switch to the smallest next piece. Deciding it now means you don't have to find willpower later.
items.hook: Wonder: what's your usual sign that you've been stuck too long?

items.title: Gommateshwara, carved from a single rock
items.body: On the hill of Vindhyagiri at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka stands a statue of Bahubali about 17 metres tall, carved from one granite boulder around 983 CE under Chavundaraya, a minister of the Western Ganga dynasty. Every twelve years or so, the Mahamastakabhisheka festival bathes it in milk, turmeric and flower petals.
items.q: Which dynasty's minister commissioned the Gommateshwara statue?
items.a: Chavundaraya, minister of the Western Ganga dynasty.

items.title: Two bright morning planets later this month
items.body: If you're up before dawn, the next few weeks are kind. Mercury reaches its greatest distance west of the Sun on 21 November, its best morning showing for a while, low in the east. Venus reaches its greatest brilliancy in the morning sky on 29 November.
items.q: On what date does Venus reach greatest brilliancy this month?
items.a: 29 November, in the morning sky.

items.title: Read it out loud
items.body: Your ear catches what your eye forgives. Reading a draft aloud, even in a whisper, reveals sentences that run out of breath, words that repeat, and rhythms that clunk. Where you stumble, the reader will too. It takes five minutes and is the cheapest edit there is.
items.hook: Wonder: why do we hear mistakes we can't see?

items.title: The quiet eye
items.body: Sport scientist Joan Vickers found that skilled performers, in golf putting, basketball free throws and more, tend to hold a steady final gaze on the target a little longer just before they move. This 'quiet eye' seems to give the brain a calm moment to set up the action, and it can be trained. A chess version might be one still look at the board before you touch a piece.

items.title: Java: joining strings without the trailing comma
items.body:
Instead of a loop that adds commas and then trims the last one, let Java do it:

String.join(", ", names)

or, from a stream:

names.stream().map(String::trim).collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]"))

The second form also adds a prefix and suffix. Both quietly handle the empty and single-item cases.
items.q: Which collector joins stream elements with a separator, prefix and suffix?
items.a: Collectors.joining(delimiter, prefix, suffix).

items.title: Petrichor has a birthday
items.body: The earthy smell after the first rain has a name, petrichor, coined in 1964 by Australian scientists Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas in the journal Nature. Part of the scent comes from geosmin, made by soil bacteria, which human noses can detect at astonishingly low concentrations.
items.q: What is the smell of rain on dry earth called?
items.a: Petrichor, a word coined in 1964.

items.title: Long-running agent harnesses on Cloudflare
items.body: Cloudflare has published reference setups for running three open agent harnesses, Codex, Exo and Nanocode, inside its Durable Objects. The point is persistence: conversation history, tool results and half-finished steps survive a restart, so an agent can pick up where it left off.

items.title: Sasikiran wins in Bavaria
items.body: Krishnan Sasikiran won the Bavarian Chess Championship at Gmund am Tegernsee with 7.5/9, first on tiebreaks ahead of Frederik Svane and Roven Vogel. FM Arun Daakshin also finished on 7.5. A neat detail: all four leaders won their final-round games with the black pieces. The open drew 548 players.

items.title: The wealth that stays
items.body: Learning is the one wealth that does not wear away; other riches are not truly wealth at all.

items.title: Gravity might tie and untie its own knots
items.body: Two physicists, Luca Comisso and Felipe Asenjo, have rewritten Einstein's equations in a form that looks like the maths of plasmas. In that view, structures in a gravitational field could break and reconnect, much as solar magnetic field lines do, passing energy into matter. It is purely theoretical so far, but they suggest it might one day show up in gravitational waves from merging black holes.
items.hook: Wonder: why does nature keep reusing the same patterns in very different places?

items.title: The QR code began on a car-parts line
items.body: In 1994, Masahiro Hara at Denso Wave, a Toyota group company, designed the QR code to track car parts faster than barcodes allowed. The black-and-white pattern was reportedly inspired by stones on a Go board. Denso chose not to enforce its patent, which is a big reason the code spread everywhere.
items.q: What was the QR code originally designed to track?
items.a: Automotive parts, at Denso Wave in 1994.

items.title: The kolam at number 14
items.body: Every morning the old woman at number 14 drew the same kolam: nine dots, one unbroken line looping around them. Every afternoon, school shoes scuffed it to dust. The boy from next door asked once why she bothered. She handed him the rice flour. He made a mess of it. The next day, a little less. By the monsoon, the line went all the way round without lifting, and she pretended not to watch.

items.title: The hypercorrection effect
items.body: Here is a kind surprise: the mistakes you were most sure about are often the easiest to fix. When people get confident answers wrong and then see the correct one, they tend to remember the correction better than for low-confidence errors (Butterfield and Metcalfe, 2001). A confident wrong guess is not wasted; it makes the right answer stand out.
items.hook: Wonder: why might surprise help a memory stick?

items.title: Robots that understand what you meant, not just what you said
items.body: Researchers at MIT and NYU have built FLEX, a system that uses large language models to infer the wider intent behind a spoken instruction for robot motion. Tell a robot not to spill coffee on the laptop, and it learns to keep drinks away from electronics in general. The work, led by Andreea Bobu, will be presented at the Conference on Robot Learning.
items.q: What does the FLEX system help a robot do?
items.a: Generalise the intent behind a natural-language instruction, like keeping drinks away from all electronics, not just one laptop.

items.title: An octopus tastes with its arms
items.body: The suckers on an octopus's arms carry chemical receptors, so touching something is also tasting it. Researchers at Harvard described these 'taste-by-touch' receptors in 2020. With much of its nervous system spread through the arms, each arm can explore a crevice fairly independently.

items.title: Gangaikonda Cholapuram, the capital named for a river
items.body: Around 1025 CE, Rajendra Chola I built a new capital in what is now Ariyalur district and named it Gangaikonda Cholapuram, 'the city of the Chola who took the Ganga', after his northern campaign. Its great Shiva temple echoes his father's Thanjavur temple but with gentler, curving lines. Today it is part of the UNESCO 'Great Living Chola Temples' listing.
items.hook: Wonder: why would a king build a temple that looks like his father's, but softer?

items.title: A to-do list before bed
items.body: If tomorrow's tasks keep circling as you try to sleep, write them down instead. In a 2018 sleep-lab study at Baylor University, people who spent five minutes writing a to-do list for the coming days fell asleep faster than those who wrote about tasks they had already finished. Paper holds the list, so your mind doesn't have to.
items.q: In the Baylor study, which kind of bedtime writing helped people fall asleep faster?
items.a: Writing a to-do list for the coming days, rather than listing tasks already done.

items.title: Gossip protocols: news that spreads like a rumour
items.body: In a big cluster, no single node can phone everyone. So each node, every second or so, picks a few random peers and swaps what it knows: who is alive, which version of a setting is current. Like village gossip, the news reaches everyone in roughly log(N) rounds, and no central server is needed. Cassandra and Consul use variations of this idea for membership and failure detection.
items.hook: Wonder: why does random chatter spread information so reliably?

items.title: Pranav V takes the World Junior Blitz title
items.body: India's Pranav V won gold in the U20 Open of the World Junior Blitz Championship in Al Ain with 10.5 points, a point clear of Eldiyar Orozbaev and Robert Piliposyan. Days earlier he had also taken silver in the rapid event. In the girls' section, Valeria Kleymenova won gold on 10 points. The festival drew 185 young players from 40 countries.
items.q: Where were the 2026 World Junior Rapid and Blitz Championships held?
items.a: Al Ain, in the United Arab Emirates.

items.title: Tuesday, early
items.body:
The milk packet waits on the step,
cold as a small promise.
A crow tests the railing, decides against it.
Somewhere a pressure cooker clears its throat.
I have not opened the day yet.
It is still folded,
like a letter I already know is kind.

items.title: A robot arm builds a truss in orbit, alone
items.body: A Caltech robotic arm, part of DARPA's NOM4D programme, has assembled pieces of a truss structure in orbit with no astronauts nearby. The experiment, called ASTRA, is working toward an 11-bay frame for a 1.4-metre reflector antenna, and has completed its third bay. With only a handful of 15-minute radio windows a day, the team solved problems using an identical twin of the robot in their lab.
items.q: How did the ASTRA team troubleshoot with so little contact time?
items.a: They tested fixes on an identical twin of the robot in their lab on the ground.

items.title: Google shares a plugin that makes coding agents write a spec first
items.body: Google has open-sourced the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM), an Apache 2.0 plugin for AI coding agents. Before any code is written, the agent drafts a specification in a Markdown file, and fresh, stateless subagents read it back to catch wrong assumptions early. Google says thousands of its engineers use it internally, though the README notes it isn't an officially supported product.
items.hook: Wonder: why might a reviewer with no memory of the conversation spot more gaps than one who was there?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Before you scroll, a small warm-up. Three questions from today's edition sit below; try each one in your head first, then check. Guessing before you know is part of how memory sticks.
items.q: In the Bavarian Championship, who won on tiebreaks with 7.5/9?
items.a: Krishnan Sasikiran, ahead of Frederik Svane and Roven Vogel.

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try to answer before you peek.
items.q: What is 'successive relearning', and which two habits does it combine?
items.a: Quizzing to one correct answer per item, repeated across several days. It combines retrieval practice and spacing.

items.title: Night rain, Monday
items.body:
The rain arrives after dinner
like a guest who knows the way,
taps the window twice,
and settles on the roof to talk
about nothing much,
for hours,
in a voice that asks for no reply.

items.title: Show the agent one finished example
items.body: Describing the output you want takes a paragraph; showing one good example takes a moment and is usually clearer. Paste a single finished sample (a commit message, a summary, a table row) and say 'match this shape'. Agents copy structure faithfully, so one example often settles format questions that a page of rules leaves open.
items.hook: Wonder: when could a single example mislead more than it helps?

items.title: Everyone sees the same Moon phase
items.body: At any moment, the Moon shows the same phase to everyone on Earth, because the phase depends only on where the Moon is relative to the Sun and Earth. What changes with where you stand is its tilt: a crescent can look like a smile near the equator and stand more upright farther north or south, and it appears flipped between the hemispheres.
items.hook: Wonder: what would the Moon's phase look like to someone standing on the Moon?

items.title: Java: validate a record in its compact constructor
items.hook: Wonder: why can you reassign the parameter but not this.lo inside a compact constructor?

items.title: At dawn
items.body: At dawn, when you are slow to rise, keep this thought ready: I am getting up to do the work of a human being. Why grumble, if I am going to do what I was made for?

items.title: Prophylaxis: ask what they want
items.body: Before choosing your move, ask one quiet question: 'If it were my opponent's turn, what would they play?' Aron Nimzowitsch called the habit of stopping that plan before it starts prophylaxis. Often the best move isn't an attack at all, just a pawn step or a rook shift that makes their best idea stop working.
items.q: What is prophylaxis in chess?
items.a: Preventing your opponent's plan before they can carry it out.

items.title: QWERTY came from a typewriter
items.body: The QWERTY layout comes from the Sholes and Glidden typewriter, sold by Remington from 1874. Christopher Latham Sholes rearranged keys over several years of prototypes. The popular story says it was meant to slow typists down; historians think it was more about keeping often-paired letters apart so the typebars jammed less, and about how telegraph operators used early machines.
items.q: Which machine gave us the QWERTY layout?
items.a: The Sholes and Glidden typewriter, sold by Remington from 1874.

items.title: Tidy one category, not one room
items.body: 'Clean the room' has no edges. 'Put away every cup' does. Pick one category (cups, chargers, clothes on the chair) and finish just that. It's easy to see when you're done, and the room often looks noticeably better after just two categories.
items.hook: Wonder: which single category would change your desk the most?

items.title: Carl Sagan was born on this day
items.body: Carl Sagan was born on 9 November 1934 in Brooklyn. He helped design the plaques and Golden Records carried by the Pioneer and Voyager spacecraft and brought the cosmos to millions through the TV series Cosmos. He also suggested Voyager 1 turn its camera homeward in 1990, giving us the 'Pale Blue Dot' image.
items.q: Which famous 1990 image did Carl Sagan push Voyager 1 to take?
items.a: The 'Pale Blue Dot', Earth seen from about 6 billion km away.

items.title: Give your character a habit
items.body: A small, repeated habit tells readers more than a paragraph of description: a man who folds every receipt into squares, a grandmother who taps the doorframe twice before leaving. Show it early, then let it change once at the moment that matters. When the habit breaks, readers feel the character break too.
items.hook: Wonder: what habit of yours would a stranger notice first?

items.title: A Pallava king who wrote a comedy
items.body: Mahendravarman I, the 7th-century Pallava king, is credited with writing Mattavilasa Prahasana ('The Farce of Drunken Revelry'), a one-act Sanskrit comedy. Its plot follows a lost begging bowl and the muddle of accusations that follows. Plays from the tradition are still staged in Kerala's Koodiyattam theatre.
items.q: What kind of play did the Pallava king Mahendravarman I write?
items.a: A one-act Sanskrit comedy (farce), Mattavilasa Prahasana.

items.title: Successive relearning
items.body: Combine two strong habits: retrieval and spacing. Quiz yourself until you get each item right once, then stop. Come back another day and do it again, and again a few days later. Research by Katherine Rawson and John Dunlosky found this 'successive relearning' gives durable memory for surprisingly little extra time, because later sessions get quicker.
items.hook: Wonder: why do the later relearning sessions take less time than the first?

items.title: Database agents for Oracle, Postgres and more
items.body: Tessell launched three agents built with Google Gemini on Google Cloud: an Ops Agent for recovery and scaling, a Governance Agent for compliance settings, and a Migrate Agent for taking inventory before a move. They cover Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL and MySQL, with an enterprise preview planned this quarter.

items.title: Venus, not Mercury, is the hottest planet
items.body: Mercury is closest to the Sun, but Venus is hotter: its surface sits around 465 °C, day and night. Its thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps heat so well that it's hot enough to melt lead. Mercury, with almost no air, swings from scorching days to freezing nights.
items.q: Which planet has the hottest surface, and why?
items.a: Venus, because its thick CO2 atmosphere traps heat.

items.title: Write-through vs write-behind caches
items.body: A write-through cache writes to the cache and the database together, so reads after writes are fresh, but every write pays the database's cost. A write-behind (write-back) cache accepts the write in the cache and flushes to the database later in batches: fast, but a crash before the flush can lose data. Choose by asking: what does losing the last few seconds of writes cost me?
items.q: What's the main risk of a write-behind cache?
items.a: Writes not yet flushed to the database can be lost if the cache fails.

items.title: The jasmine seller's last string
items.body: At eight, the jasmine seller had one string left, too short to sell. She looked at the bus stop: a tired nurse, a boy with a schoolbag, an old man with a cloth bag of onions. She cut the string into three and handed them out without a word. The bus came. Three people rode home smelling of flowers and didn't know why they were smiling.

items.title: Bullet Grandpa takes a game from Dubov
items.body: In the Season 1 final of Chess.com's 100-0 Project, Arizona amateur Josh Smith, known online as Bullet Grandpa, won a game against super-GM Daniil Dubov in game 28. That one win meant there would be no 100-0 sweep. A small, happy reminder that every game starts level.

items.title: Rubin finds a world that orbits backwards
items.body: EarthSky reports that the Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found an object beyond Neptune on a retrograde orbit, travelling around the Sun in the opposite direction to the planets. Almost everything in the solar system circles the same way, a leftover from the spinning disc it formed in, so the backward ones are clues to old gravitational nudges.
items.hook: Wonder: what could flip a small world's orbit around?

items.title: Ripe fruit
items.body: To speak harsh words when kind ones are at hand is like picking unripe fruit while ripe fruit hangs on the same tree.

items.title: Hamming's weekend problem
items.body: At Bell Labs in the late 1940s, Richard Hamming ran long jobs on a relay computer over weekends. When the machine detected an error, it simply dropped his job, and he'd come back on Monday to nothing. Annoyed, he asked: if a machine can detect an error, why can't it fix one? His 1950 paper on error-correcting codes answered that, and Hamming codes still help protect data in memory today.
items.q: What question led Richard Hamming to invent error-correcting codes?
items.a: If the machine can detect an error, why can't it locate and correct it?

items.title: Watching an agent from your phone
items.body: DigitalOcean introduced Cuttlefish, an iPhone app for its Managed Agents. You can follow an agent's live session, approve or deny the tools it wants to use, steer it, or stop it. Managed Agents is still in public preview.
items.hook: Wonder: which agent actions would you always want to approve yourself?

items.title: Measure chores in songs
items.body: Minutes are abstract; songs are not. Put on one song and do the dishes until it ends. A song is about three or four minutes, has a clear finish line, and makes time something you can hear. If you want to keep going, play another; if not, you've still done a full song's worth.
items.q: Why can a song work better than a minute timer for starting a chore?
items.a: It makes time audible and gives a clear, short finish line.

items.title: Sound is faster underwater
items.body: In air at room temperature, sound travels about 343 metres per second. In seawater it travels about 1,500 metres per second, more than four times as fast, because water is far stiffer, which more than makes up for being denser. That's one reason whale calls can carry across whole ocean basins.
items.hook: Wonder: is sound even faster through steel?

items.title: Poompuhar, the port at the river's mouth
items.body: Poompuhar, also called Kaveripattinam, sat where the Kaveri meets the sea and was a major early Chola port. Sangam-era works such as Pattinappalai and the Silappatikaram describe its busy markets, warehouses and ships. The Silappatikaram's heroine Kannagi and her husband Kovalan begin their story in this city.
items.q: Which Chola port city, at the Kaveri's mouth, opens the Silappatikaram?
items.a: Poompuhar (Kaveripattinam).

items.title: The production effect
items.body: Words you say out loud are remembered better than words you read silently. Researchers call this the production effect: saying, writing or typing an item makes it stand out from the rest. It works best when you produce only the key items, not everything, so the important lines become the distinctive ones.
items.hook: Wonder: why does the effect shrink if you read every single word aloud?

items.title: Vector clocks: who knew what, when
items.body: A Lamport clock gives one number per event, which orders events but can't tell you whether two updates were concurrent. A vector clock keeps one counter per node. Each node bumps its own entry on every event and takes the element-wise maximum when it receives a message. If every entry of A is less than or equal to B's, then A happened before B; if neither dominates, the two were concurrent, and you have a real conflict to resolve.
items.q: With vector clocks, how do you tell two events were concurrent?
items.a: Neither vector is less-than-or-equal to the other in every entry.

items.title: No moon
items.body:
Tonight the moon took a day off.
The sky, unsupervised,
let every small star speak.
I stood on the terrace a long time,
listening with my eyes.

items.title: India heads to the Asian Nations Cup
items.body: The Asian Nations Chess Cup runs in Abu Dhabi from 9 to 18 November. India's squad includes GMs Nihal Sarin, Aravindh Chithambaram, V Pranav and M Pranesh, with WGM Vantika Agarwal, WIMs Guntaka Aamukta and Sirin Kalyani, WFM Shubhi Gupta and WCM Modipalli Deekshitha.
items.hook: Wonder: in a team event, why does board order matter so much?

items.title: A 284-billion-parameter model on a CPU-only machine
items.body: An open-source project called llama-modchip squeezes DeepSeek V4-Flash, a 284B-parameter model, into about 57 GB using a custom quantisation of roughly 1.7 bits per weight. Its authors report it running on 64 GB machines with no GPU (AMD Zen 5, Apple Silicon and ARM64) at around 9 to 15 tokens per second. Big models are slowly becoming things you can run at home.
items.q: About how many bits per weight does llama-modchip use to fit a 284B model in ~57 GB?
items.a: Roughly 1.7 bits per weight.

items.title: New Moon tonight: the darkest skies of the month
items.body: The Moon is new on 9 November, so the next few evenings are moonless and dark. EarthSky's November guide notes Mars and Jupiter drawing closer together in the sky. A clear night this week is a good one to step outside, let your eyes adjust for ten minutes, and see how many more stars appear.
items.hook: Wonder: why does a new Moon rise and set with the Sun, so it never lights the night?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try to answer before you peek.
items.q: What happens to effort as a goal comes into view, and what's that called?
items.a: Effort tends to speed up near the finish. It's called the goal-gradient effect.

items.title: Long enough
items.body: Life is long enough, if you know how to use it.
items.who: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life (own rendering)

items.title: Ledger of a slow evening
items.body:
Credit: one long shadow of the neem.
Credit: the neighbour's radio, low.
Debit: nothing.
Carried forward: the last of the light,
which I did not spend,
only watched.

items.title: Ask the agent what it assumed
items.body: When an agent finishes a task, ask one more question: 'List the assumptions you made that I didn't state.' Hidden guesses (which file, which time zone, which version) are where most quiet mistakes live, and naming them takes seconds.

items.title: Java: sort by more than one thing
items.body:
Comparators chain cleanly:

people.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::city)
    .thenComparing(Person::age, Comparator.reverseOrder()));

This sorts by city, then oldest first within each city. Java's List.sort is stable, so items that are equal on every key keep their original order.
items.hook: Wonder: why does a stable sort let you build multi-key sorts one key at a time?

items.title: CSIRAC, the computer that played music
items.body: CSIRAC, Australia's first stored-program computer, was among the first computers anywhere to play music. Programmers made its speaker pulse at chosen rates to form notes, and it played tunes such as the 'Colonel Bogey March' for an audience in 1951. Today the machine is kept at Museums Victoria in Melbourne.
items.q: Which early computer, now in Melbourne, played music in 1951?
items.a: CSIRAC, Australia's first stored-program computer.

items.title: An admin hour for the small stuff
items.body: Tiny chores (a form, a bill, a reply) each cost a switch of attention. Collect them in one list and give them a single weekly slot, with music and a cup of something. One hour of small wins in a row feels lighter than twenty interruptions scattered across the week.

items.title: A second crazyhouse crown for Awatramani
items.body: Janak Awatramani won the 2026 Chess.com Crazyhouse Championship, his second title in the event. In crazyhouse, captured pieces switch sides and can be dropped back onto the board, so games stay lively to the end.

items.title: The lotus pond of Sittanavasal
items.body: In a Jain cave temple at Sittanavasal, in Pudukkottai district, faint old paintings still cover the ceiling: a lotus pond with fish, ducks, elephants and people gathering flowers. Dated by scholars to somewhere between the 7th and 9th centuries, they are among the oldest surviving paintings in Tamil Nadu.
items.hook: Wonder: what made those pigments last more than a thousand years on a cave ceiling?

items.title: Jupiter spins in under ten hours
items.body: The largest planet has the shortest day in the solar system: Jupiter turns once in about 9 hours 56 minutes. The fast spin flattens it slightly, so it is noticeably wider at the equator than from pole to pole.
items.q: How long is a day on Jupiter?
items.a: About 9 hours 56 minutes, the shortest of any planet.

items.title: End the scene on a turn
items.body: A useful test for any scene: is something different at the end compared with the start? A hope becomes a doubt, a secret becomes shared, a stranger becomes an ally. If nothing has turned, the scene may be scenery. Keep the best image and fold it into a scene that moves.
items.q: What simple test tells you a scene is earning its place?
items.a: Something has turned: a value or situation has changed between the scene's start and end.

items.title: The Pacific is wider than the Moon
items.body: At its widest, from Indonesia to the coast of Colombia, the Pacific Ocean stretches about 19,800 km. That's more than five times the Moon's diameter of about 3,475 km.
items.hook: Wonder: how many Moons could you line up across the Pacific?

items.title: Meta brings Active Memory to Muse users
items.body: Meta is rolling out smaller models derived from its Muse Wonder series to all Muse and Meta AI users, keeping the larger Wonder Full for paid subscribers. The update adds Active Memory, which keeps useful information across conversations, and Active Focus, which helps a task pick up where it left off after an interruption.

items.title: Java: counting with Map.merge
items.q: What does map.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum) do when k is missing?
items.a: It puts 1 for k. Otherwise it adds 1 to the existing count.

items.title: The doorway effect
items.body: Ever walked into a room and forgotten why? Experiments by Gabriel Radvansky and colleagues found that passing through a doorway makes people forget slightly more than walking the same distance in one room. Event boundaries seem to file away the previous 'scene'. Walking back to where you started often brings the thought back.
items.hook: Wonder: does turning a page in a book count as a doorway?

items.title: Think, then begin
items.body:
Think it through, then begin.
To begin and only then think
is where the fault lies.

items.title: Checks, captures, threats
items.body: Before every move in a sharp position, scan in a fixed order: every check, then every capture, then every threat, for both sides. The habit is boring, and that is why it works. It stops your eye from locking onto the one move it likes and missing the forcing reply.
items.q: What's the order in the forcing-move scan?
items.a: Checks, captures, threats, for you and for your opponent.

items.title: Tennis for Two (1958)
items.body: In October 1958, physicist William Higinbotham set up a game for visitors' day at Brookhaven National Laboratory: an analog computer drew a tennis court side-on on an oscilloscope screen, and two players used knobs and buttons to hit a glowing ball over the net. Visitors queued to play. It is often counted among the first video games, made four years before Spacewar!
items.hook: Wonder: what's the smallest set of rules that still feels like a game?

items.title: The stamp collector's duplicates
items.body: Every Sunday the old man sorted his stamps, and every Sunday he set the duplicates aside in an envelope marked LATER. The girl next door asked what Later meant. He thought about it and handed her the envelope. She came back the next week with an album of her own and one stamp he had never seen. He found a fresh envelope and, after a moment, wrote NOW.

items.title: A farewell to Swift
items.body: After nearly 22 years watching the sky, NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory re-entered Earth's atmosphere on 4 November over North Sumatra. Its orbit had sunk faster than expected during the recent solar maximum. To mark its retirement, NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day shared a mosaic built from Swift's ultraviolet images, a small thank-you for a career spent catching the universe's brightest flashes.

items.title: Say the time out loud
items.body: A vague 'I'll send it later' slips away easily. A spoken 'I'll send it by 4' to a colleague or friend works better. A specific time plus another person who heard it gives you a gentle outside anchor, so you don't have to hold the deadline in your head alone.

items.title: A giraffe's neck has seven bones
items.body: A giraffe has seven neck vertebrae, the same number as you, a mouse or a whale. Each of the giraffe's is just much longer, up to about 25 cm.
items.q: How many neck vertebrae does a giraffe have?
items.a: Seven, the same as almost every mammal, including humans.

items.title: Google's ADK 2.14 moves features to stable
items.body: Google released Agent Development Kit 2.14.0, a major version that moves several experimental pieces to stable: execution environments, A2A (agent-to-agent) protocol support, evaluation modules and the core runtime. It also adds multi-run evaluation, so you can run the same test several times and see how consistent an agent is.
items.hook: Wonder: if an agent passes a test once, how many reruns before you trust it?

items.title: A temple without brick, timber, metal or mortar
items.body: At Mandagapattu, near Villupuram in Tamil Nadu, the Pallava king Mahendravarman I left an early 7th-century inscription in a small cave shrine. It proudly says the temple was made without brick, timber, metal or mortar. It was cut straight from the rock, an early step toward the rock-cut wonders later made at Mamallapuram.
items.q: What four materials does the Mandagapattu inscription say were not used?
items.a: Brick, timber, metal and mortar. The shrine was cut from living rock.

items.title: Hedged requests: ask twice, politely
items.body: Slow outliers dominate tail latency. A hedged request sends a query to one replica and, if no answer arrives within a short delay (say the 95th-percentile time), sends the same query to a second replica and uses whichever reply comes first. In Google's 'The Tail at Scale' (Dean & Barroso, 2013), this cut a benchmark's 99.9th-percentile latency from 1,800 ms to 74 ms while adding only about 2% more requests.
items.hook: Wonder: why does waiting a little before the second request cost far less than sending both at once?

items.title: Seniors halfway in Serbia
items.body: The FIDE World Senior Championships in Vrnjačka Banja are past the halfway mark, with six rounds left and the final round on 14 November. In the Women 65+ section, WGM Galina Strutinskaya has a perfect 5/5. In Women 50+, Monica Calzetta Ruiz leads by half a point over Pia Cramling, and the Open 65+ has a five-way tie that includes Keith Arkell.

items.title: The goal-gradient effect
items.body: We tend to speed up as a goal comes into view. In a 2006 study, coffee-shop customers bought coffees faster the closer their loyalty card got to a free drink. A card with 12 stamps, two already filled in, was completed faster than a blank 10-stamp card, even though both needed ten purchases.
items.q: Why did the 12-stamp card with two free stamps get finished faster?
items.a: It felt further along. Visible progress pulls effort forward (the goal-gradient effect).

items.title: Monday, 6 am
items.body:
The milk packet waits on the step,
cool as a promise.
A crow tries one word, then another.
The week hasn't happened yet —
for now it is only this:
a tap running,
the kettle clearing its throat.

items.title: Microsoft open-sources a package manager for agents
items.body: Microsoft released APM (Agent Package Manager) under the MIT licence. You list an agent's skills, prompts, instructions, plugins and MCP servers in an apm.yml file, and APM installs them into supported tools such as GitHub Copilot, Claude Code and Cursor, with a lockfile so a setup can be reproduced exactly.
items.q: What does APM's lockfile give you?
items.a: A reproducible agent setup: the same skills and tool versions every time it's installed.

items.title: A mountain at the Moon's south pole
items.body: NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day for 7 November showed the De Gerlache–Kocher massif, a mountain block rising about 4 km near the Moon's south pole. The photo, taken from Earth on 31 October, caught it at a lucky angle thanks to libration, the Moon's slow wobble. Nearby craters that never see sunlight probably hold water ice, and the massif has been considered as a landing site for future Artemis crews.
items.hook: Wonder: how can a crater on a sunlit world stay dark for billions of years?

items.title: Clothesline, afternoon
items.body:
Shirts lift their arms
to nobody in particular.
A dupatta practises being a flag.
By four o'clock
everything smells of sun
and is ready to come home.

items.title: Let the agent write its own checklist
items.body: For a multi-step task, ask the agent to first write a short checklist of what 'done' includes, then tick items off as it works. The list becomes something you can read at a glance, and a skipped step shows up as an unticked box rather than a surprise.

items.title: Hippos make their own sunscreen
items.body: Hippos secrete a reddish-orange fluid from their skin that's often called 'blood sweat', though it's neither blood nor sweat. Its pigments absorb ultraviolet light and seem to help protect their skin.
items.hook: Wonder: what other animals carry their own sun protection?

items.title: The pre-mortem
items.body: Before starting a project, imagine it's a year later and things didn't go well. Each person writes down why. Psychologist Gary Klein's technique makes it easier to voice quiet doubts, because you're explaining an imagined past rather than criticising a plan.
items.q: In a pre-mortem, what do you imagine before starting?
items.a: That the project has already gone badly, then list the reasons why.

items.title: Least connections vs round robin
items.body: Round robin hands requests out in turn, which is fair only if every request costs the same. When some requests are slow, 'least connections' sends new work to the server currently doing the least, so one stuck server doesn't keep receiving its share of traffic.
items.hook: Wonder: what goes wrong if a 'least connections' balancer sees a brand-new server with zero connections?

items.title: Good bishop, bad bishop
items.body: A bishop is 'bad' when your own pawns sit on its colour and block its diagonals, and 'good' when they're on the other colour. A simple habit: when you fix pawns in place, put them on the opposite colour to your remaining bishop.
items.q: What makes a bishop 'bad'?
items.a: Your own pawns are fixed on the same colour squares, blocking it.

items.title: Confine yourself to the present.
items.body: Confine thyself to the present.

items.title: Muziris, the pepper port
items.body: Muziris, on the Kerala coast, was one of the great ports of the ancient Indian Ocean trade. A first-century Greek sailing guide, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes ships coming there for pepper. Excavations at Pattanam, near Kodungallur, are widely thought to have found part of it.
items.hook: Wonder: how did monsoon winds decide when ships could sail to Muziris and back?

items.title: Venus Express turns 21
items.body: On 8 November 2005, Europe launched Venus Express, its first mission to Venus. Over more than nine years it watched a swirling vortex at the planet's south pole, found possible signs of active volcanoes, and showed that Venus has auroras of its own.
items.q: Which mission, launched on 8 November 2005, found that Venus has its own auroras?
items.a: ESA's Venus Express.

items.title: Pong's one-line manual
items.body: Atari's 1972 Pong arcade cabinet came with possibly the shortest instructions in gaming: 'Avoid missing ball for high score.' Its simplicity was part of the appeal; anyone could walk up and play.
items.q: What did the original Pong cabinet's instructions say?
items.a: 'Avoid missing ball for high score.'

items.title: The mapmaker's blank corner
items.body: Every map the old mapmaker sold had one small blank corner. Customers complained; he only smiled. Years later a girl brought one back with the corner filled in: a lane, a well, a tree she had drawn after walking there herself. He framed it, and from then on he charged a little less for maps with bigger corners.

items.title: OpenAI's BioBasicsBench: agents meet messy lab data
items.body: OpenAI introduced BioBasicsBench, a 100-task benchmark that checks how well AI agents read raw, untidy wet-lab results and notice when an experiment looks off. It measures careful interpretation rather than textbook recall.
items.hook: Wonder: what would a good 'that looks odd' instinct look like in an agent?

items.title: A sea lion that keeps the beat
items.body: A California sea lion named Ronan learned to bob her head in time to music, and then kept the beat to songs she had never heard, at new tempos. Researchers had long thought rhythm-keeping needed vocal mimicry; Ronan showed it isn't so simple.
items.q: What was surprising about Ronan the sea lion?
items.a: She could keep time to music, even new songs and tempos, though sea lions aren't known vocal mimics.

items.title: Self-explanation
items.body: When you read a worked solution, pause at each step and say why it follows. Learners who explain steps to themselves, even silently, tend to understand and transfer the idea better than those who just reread. The gaps you notice while explaining are exactly the bits to study.
items.hook: Wonder: which step in something you 'know' would you struggle to justify out loud?

items.title: Chinese Rapid Championship reaches its final four
items.body: The Chinese Rapid Championship's quarterfinals were decided, some only in blitz tiebreaks. Yu Yangyi, Xiao Tong, Xu Xiangyu and Lu Shanglei go through to the semifinals.

items.title: Ask the question before you open the tab
items.body: Research can become an endless corridor. Before searching, write the one question you're answering and what 'answered' looks like. When you find it, close the tabs. Anything else interesting goes on a 'later' list, not into this session.
items.hook: Wonder: how often does a five-minute lookup become an hour, and what was the original question?

items.title: Java: fail-fast iterators
items.body: Change an ArrayList while a for-each loop walks it and you'll usually get a ConcurrentModificationException. That's deliberate: the iterator notices the list's modification count changed and stops early rather than giving quietly wrong results. To remove while iterating, use iterator.remove() or list.removeIf(...).
items.q: What's the safe way to remove elements from an ArrayList based on a condition?
items.a: list.removeIf(condition), or iterator.remove() inside an explicit iterator loop.

items.title: Northern Taurids peak around 12 November
items.body: The Northern Taurid meteor shower peaks around 12 November, with roughly five meteors an hour under dark skies. Taurids are slow and known for occasional bright fireballs, and the Leonids follow before dawn on 17–18 November.
items.q: Which shower peaks around 12 November, known for its slow, bright fireballs?
items.a: The Northern Taurids.

items.title: Save the weight for the end of the sentence
items.body: English readers lean toward the last words of a sentence. Put the familiar part first and the new or striking part last. 'The letter she'd waited a year for came on a Tuesday' lands on an ordinary day; 'On a Tuesday, the letter came: the one she'd waited a year for' lands on the wait.
items.q: Where in a sentence does emphasis naturally fall in English?
items.a: Near the end, so place the new or important idea there.

items.title: A whole cliff turned into a story
items.body: At Mamallapuram, Pallava-era sculptors carved a huge open-air relief across two boulders, about 27 metres long and 9 metres high. Often called Arjuna's Penance or the Descent of the Ganga, it is crowded with gods, sages, hunters and life-sized elephants, and a natural cleft down the middle stands in for the river.
items.hook: Wonder: how did sculptors plan a scene that size before the first chisel stroke?

items.title: Vercel Labs' agent-desktop reads the screen as structure
items.body: Vercel Labs released agent-desktop, an open-source command-line tool that lets AI agents operate desktop apps on macOS, Windows and Linux. Instead of reading screenshots, it uses the operating system's accessibility tree, which uses fewer tokens and doesn't take over your cursor.
items.q: What does agent-desktop use instead of screenshots to understand an app?
items.a: The operating system's accessibility tree.

items.title: Small help, seen large
items.body: Though the help given is as small as a millet seed, those who know its worth see it as large as a palm tree.

items.title: On Venus the Sun rises in the west
items.body: Venus spins in the opposite direction to most planets, and very slowly. Stand on its surface (if you could see through the clouds) and the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east.
items.hook: Wonder: how might a planet end up spinning backwards in the first place?

items.title: Memory that was woven by hand
items.body: From the 1950s to the 1970s, many computers stored data in magnetic core memory: tiny ferrite rings threaded onto a grid of wires, often by hand. The Apollo guidance computer went further with 'core rope' memory, where its programs were literally woven: a wire passing through a core meant 1, around it meant 0.
items.q: In Apollo's core rope memory, how was a 1 vs a 0 encoded?
items.a: By whether a wire passed through a core (1) or bypassed it (0).

items.title: A checklist for the routine you 'already know'
items.body: Pilots run checklists for things they've done thousands of times, because familiarity doesn't stop a skipped step. A short, visible list for your morning or leaving-the-house routine takes the remembering off your working memory. Tick it; don't trust it to your head.
items.hook: Wonder: which daily routine of yours has a step that quietly goes missing?

items.title: The method of loci
items.body: Place each thing you want to remember at a spot along a route you know well: the gate, the stairs, the kitchen shelf. To recall, walk the route in your mind. It works because spatial memory is old, strong and orderly, so it lends its structure to facts that have none.
items.q: What does the method of loci borrow to organise new memories?
items.a: A familiar physical route: spatial memory gives the items an order and a place.

items.title: Aadik Theophane Leninn becomes India's newest IM
items.body: At the 1st Chola Chess GM tournament in Chennai, 14-year-old Aadik Theophane Leninn secured his final International Master norm with a round to spare. Going into the last round, GMs Pranesh M and Vitaliy Bernadskiy and Pa Iniyan shared the lead on 6 points.
items.q: Which Chennai event saw Aadik Theophane Leninn complete his IM title?
items.a: The 1st Chola Chess GM 2026.

items.title: Power cut, 9 pm
items.body:
The fan slows to a stop
and the street remembers its crickets.
Someone finds a candle,
someone finds a story,
and for an hour
the whole house sits in one room.
